posts.text: What if the people businesses are reluctant to hire are some of the talent they’re missing out on? There can be a perception that employing someone who has experienced homelessness, or is at risk of it, will require more time, support and investment. , CEO ofand UK Chair of Homewards’ New Employment Opportunities Network, believes employers should look at the other side of that equation. With the right recruitment, onboarding and ongoing support, businesses can open themselves up to a more diverse pool of talent, help people stay and progress in work and strengthen retention. That matters to individual businesses. But it matters to the economy too. With around one in eight young people not in education, employment or training, businesses have an opportunity to be part of the solution by giving people who might otherwise be overlooked a genuine route into sustainable work. NEON exists to help make that easier, connecting employers to local organisations that support both the business and the young person before and after they start work. sat down withto discuss why this isn’t simply about social responsibility. It’s about seeing potential where others see risk. Full episode in the comments 👇 Follow, hosted by, for conversations about the future of work and careers nobody else is having. … more

posts.text: Job quality in Latin America and the Caribbean has reached a record high, surpassing pre-pandemic levels for the first time. Important progress, but challenges remain. The’s 2026 BetterIndex highlights where we need to focus: making formal employment simpler and less costly, boosting productivity, and strengthening social protection. Menos de una de cada tres personas en edad de trabajar tiene un empleo formal con seguridad social, y los jóvenes enfrentan dificultades particulares para acceder a empleos de calidad. posts.text: 30 Sekunden Video. Und plötzlich fallen Scammer und Blender durchs Raster. Bevor ein Kandidat einen unserer Kunden trifft, gibt es in unserem Auswahlprozess einen einfachen ersten Schritt: ein 30-Sekunden-Video über sich. Nicht zur Präsentation beim Kunden. Nicht, um das Aussehen zu beurteilen. Und schon gar nicht als Ersatz für die technische Prüfung. Es geht um Kommunikation. In verteilten Engineering-Teams ist technisches Können nur ein Teil der Gleichung. Man muss eine technische Entscheidung klar erklären können, ein Problem ansprechen, bevor es zum Blocker wird, die richtigen Fragen stellen und komplexe Themen für Menschen verständlich machen, die nicht denselben fachlichen Hintergrund haben. Das zeigt kein Lebenslauf. Und ein Coding-Test zeigt es auch nicht zuverlässig. Das Video leistet außerdem etwas, womit wir anfangs nicht gerechnet haben: Es filtert früh. Wir haben schon Kandidaten im Bademantel oder Schlafanzug im Interview gehabt. Wir hatten Bewerber, die angaben, in der EU zu leben und geboren zu sein, aber keine einzige EU-Landessprache beherrschten und ihre Antworten von einem zweiten Bildschirm ablasen. Es geht uns nicht um Hochglanz. Aber Professionalität und ein echtes Gespräch zählen, und 30 Sekunden reichen oft, um zu sehen, ob beides da ist. Wer diesen Schritt besteht, bekommt von uns mehr: Jeder Kandidat erhält ein auf die jeweilige Stelle zugeschnittenes Vorbereitungsdokument und ein weiteres persönliches Gespräch mit uns, damit er gut vorbereitet und entspannt ins finale Kundengespräch geht. Denn in Teams, die über Länder, Zeitzonen und Kulturen hinweg arbeiten, ist Kommunikation kein Soft Skill. Es ist ein absolutes Must-Have. Bei Scorpion Power, Teil der POWERCODE GROUP, nutzen wir strukturierte Auswahlverfahren, um Engineers zu finden, die technisch überzeugen und in verteilten Teams gut kommunizieren. 30 Sekunden zeigen oft mehr, als ein Lebenslauf je könnte. posts.text: NIS2 to nie tylko kolejny obowiązek regulacyjny. To szansa, aby potraktować cyberbezpieczeństwo jako element odporności biznesowej, równie istotny jak płynność, ryzyko kredytowe czy ciągłość działalności. Najlepiej przygotowane organizacje nie muszą być tymi, które wydają najwięcej. Kluczowe jest zrozumienie, co należy chronić, jakie ryzyka mogą zagrozić działalności oraz czy wdrożone zabezpieczenia rzeczywiście działają. Kiedy zarząd ostatnio rozmawiał o ryzyku cybernetycznym obok ryzyka płynności lub kredytowego? NIS2 is more than another regulatory obligation. It is an opportunity to treat cybersecurity as a core element of business resilience, alongside liquidity, credit risk and going concern. The best-prepared organisations will not necessarily be those that spend the most. What matters is understanding what needs to be protected, which risks could disrupt the business and whether the safeguards in place actually work. When did your board last discuss cyber risk alongside liquidity or credit risk? … more Show translation Why I See NIS2 as Genuinely Good News Aleksandra Motławska

posts.text: 📢 WE ARE HIRING – ACCOUNTING & TAX SPECIALIST Kami sedang mencari kandidat profesional dan berpengalaman untuk bergabung bersama tim kami sebagai Accounting & Tax Specialist. Posisi ini bertanggung jawab dalam mengelola proses akuntansi, pembukuan, penyusunan laporan keuangan, serta administrasi dan kepatuhan perpajakan perusahaan. Selain itu, posisi ini juga bertanggung jawab melakukan monitoring dan pemeriksaan laporan serta dokumen keuangan dari lokasi operasional perusahaan. 📍 Lokasi Penempatan: PIK 1, Jakarta Utara Tanggung Jawab Pekerjaan: 1. Mengelola proses pembukuan dan pencatatan transaksi akuntansi perusahaan secara akurat dan sistematis. 2. Melakukan pemeriksaan jurnal, buku besar, rekonsiliasi bank, serta memastikan kesesuaian pencatatan transaksi keuangan. 3. Menyusun dan menganalisis laporan keuangan bulanan dan tahunan, termasuk laporan laba rugi, neraca, dan laporan arus kas. 4. Mengelola administrasi perpajakan perusahaan, termasuk perhitungan, pembayaran, dan pelaporan pajak sesuai peraturan perpajakan yang berlaku. 5. Memastikan kepatuhan perusahaan terhadap peraturan perpajakan serta mengikuti perubahan ketentuan perpajakan yang relevan. 6. Melakukan pemeriksaan dan verifikasi dokumen transaksi, invoice, bukti pengeluaran, serta dokumen pendukung akuntansi lainnya. 7. Melakukan monitoring dan rekonsiliasi laporan keuangan serta penggunaan dana operasional dari lokasi pertambangan. 8. Melakukan kunjungan berkala ke site Bombana untuk memeriksa kesesuaian transaksi, dokumen pendukung, laporan pengeluaran, dan pencatatan keuangan di lokasi. 9. Berkoordinasi dengan tim operasional dan pihak terkait untuk memastikan kelengkapan serta keakuratan laporan keuangan. Kualifikasi: 1. Memiliki pengalaman kerja minimal 5 tahun di bidang Accounting dan Tax. 2. Memiliki pemahaman yang kuat mengenai standar akuntansi dan penyusunan laporan keuangan. 3. Menguasai proses pembukuan, jurnal akuntansi, rekonsiliasi, dan analisis laporan keuangan. 4. Memahami peraturan perpajakan di Indonesia, termasuk PPh, PPN, serta kewajiban pelaporan pajak perusahaan. 5. Memiliki pengalaman dalam pengelolaan administrasi dan pelaporan pajak perusahaan. 6. Mampu mengoperasikan Microsoft Excel dengan baik dan terbiasa menggunakan software akuntansi. 7. Mampu bekerja secara mandiri serta bertanggung jawab terhadap ketepatan dan keakuratan laporan. 8. Bersedia melakukan perjalanan dinas ke Bombana, Sulawesi Tenggara secara berkala. Kualifikasi Tambahan (Menjadi Nilai Plus): 1. Memiliki pengalaman di industri pertambangan atau perusahaan dengan operasional multi-lokasi. 2. Memiliki pengalaman dalam internal audit, financial control, dan pemeriksaan laporan keuangan. 3. Memiliki sertifikasi Brevet Pajak A dan B. 📩 Cara Melamar: Kandidat yang memenuhi kualifikasi dapat mengirimkan CV terbaru melalui: Email: [email hidden] Subjek: Accounting & Tax Specialist – Nama Lengkap

posts.text: Ný grein eftir mig á Vísi: Íslensk bókhaldsgögn eiga heima innan Evrópu Nú liggur fyrir frumvarp að nýjum heildarlögum um bókhald sem á að leysa af hólmi lögin frá 1994. Í því er fallið frá kröfunni um að bókhaldsgögn séu geymd á Íslandi. Það er rétt skref, því skýjalausnir eru orðnar almenn regla. Mér finnst þó vanta eitt. Lögin þurfa að ná yfir það hvar gögnin eru unnin, ekki bara hvar þau eru geymd. Þegar gervigreind er farin að bóka reikninga og stemma af skiptir enn meira máli hvert gögnin eru send til úrvinnslu. Í þessu samhengi snýst Evrópa ekki um landafræði heldur um lögsögu. Innan EES gilda GDPR og evrópsk lög. Ef gögnin eru unnin utan EES ná íslensk og evrópsk lög hvorki yfir afritun, varðveislu né aðgang erlendra stjórnvalda. Í greininni legg ég til þrennt: 1️⃣ Geymsla og úrvinnsla innan EES, með aðlögunartíma. 2️⃣ Skyldurnar liggi hjá skráðum veitendum bókhaldskerfa en ekki hjá litlum fyrirtækjum, og ekki megi semja þær burt. 3️⃣ Allar sjálfvirkar tillögur verði rekjanlegar: Frá hvaða fylgiskjali, hvað var gert sjálfvirkt, hver breytti og hver samþykkti. Það var gaman að sjá að fleiri umsagnir um frumvarpið koma inn á sömu atriði, meðal annars frá Uniconta og Óskari Sigurðssyni hjá Accountant, en ég skrifa útfrá reynslu minni sem tæknistjóri. posts.text: Sufit może stać się jednym z najbardziej wyrazistych elementów architektury wnętrza — budować jego tożsamość, przyciągać uwagę i zmieniać atmosferę za pomocą światła. W NEWMAT Polska tworzymy sufity i panele sufitowe z wykorzystaniem specjalnych tkanin kinetycznych 3D. Ich połączenie z odpowiednio zaprojektowanym oświetleniem LED pozwala uzyskać przestrzenne efekty wizualne, świetlne wzory i wrażenie głębi. Za efektem stoją trzy współpracujące elementy: ▪️ Tkanina kinetyczna 3D, która nadaje światłu wyjątkowy efekt przestrzenny. ▪️ Dobór i rozmieszczenie źródeł LED — w tym modułów oraz taśm — kształtujące wzór świetlny. ▪️ System sterowania oświetleniem, który pozwala zmieniać kolory, programować sekwencje i tworzyć płynne przejścia. Kolor pochodzi ze źródeł LED. Przy zastosowaniu odpowiedniego systemu każdy z prezentowanych paneli może być podświetlany w dowolnie wybranej barwie. Jeden projekt zyskuje dzięki temu wiele odsłon — od subtelnego światła po dynamiczne kompozycje kolorystyczne. To możliwości dla architektów i inwestorów projektujących hotelowe lobby, recepcje, restauracje, przestrzenie komercyjne oraz indywidualne wnętrza. Rozwiązanie można wykorzystać zarówno w sufitach i panelach sufitowych, jak i w kompozycjach ściennych. Projektujesz przestrzeń, w której światło ma odgrywać główną rolę? Porozmawiajmy o możliwościach zastosowania tkanin kinetycznych 3D w Twojej koncepcji. NEWMAT Polska — przekształcamy światło w sztukę. #NEWMATPolska #ArchitekturaWnętrz #ProjektowanieOświetlenia #TkaninyKinetyczne3D #SufityNapinane #oświetlenie #akustyka #design

posts.text: 💡 If you’re thinking, “I’ll pick my job search back up in January,” you may be sitting out opportunities worth exploring right now. The calendar turning to November doesn’t mean hiring stops. Companies still have full-time positions to fill, teams that need support, and business goals that won’t wait until the new year. Some hiring processes will slow around holiday schedules. Others are moving with urgency to get someone in place before January. My advice? Stay in the conversation and go beyond hitting “Apply.” With so much of the application process happening online, a thoughtful human connection can help someone understand the experience behind your résumé. → Find the recruiter supporting the role. → Reach out to the hiring manager with a brief, relevant introduction. → Look for a former colleague, alumni connection, or someone you know at the company. → Ask thoughtful questions about the opportunity and the team. 📲 Make your outreach specific. Share what caught your attention, how your experience connects, and what you’d like to learn. Give the person something meaningful to respond to. Applying is still part of the process. Building relationships deserves a place in your strategy, too. You don’t have to wait for a new year to make your next move. #hiringnow #financejobs #openroles #hotjobs #LifeatSIG #Recruiterlife … more

posts.text: Looking for a real career horror story? 👻 It isn’t a server crash on a Friday afternoon or a typo sent to 10,000 subscribers. It’s "Ghosting"—and it's haunting today's job market. Whether it’s a candidate disappearing before a final interview or an employer leaving a professional in limbo after three rounds, ghosting hurts everyone. If you need to reschedule, communicate early. The best professional relationships are built on respect, not disappearing acts. posts.text: A gap on your CV isn't the problem. An unexplained gap is. Humans have this psychological quirk where we fill gaps in information with the worst-case scenario. Many contractors, especially, take lengthier breaks between demanding projects to live their lives: spend time with family, travel, develop their skills. It might seem silly or unprofessional to include this on your CV, but, if a hiring manager has never spoken to you, a blank stretch on your CV can become 'couldn’t find work' or 'left on bad terms', when the reality is usually different. You may have been working toward professional qualifications, building relationships for future work, travelling, honing soft skills. But, the hiring manager won't know unless you tell them: ❌ [blank gap, Mar 2025 – Oct 2025] ✅ Career break, Mar 2025 – Oct 2025: completed CISI qualification in July and spent time with family. (Swap in what’s true for you. Don’t invent anything, because it’ll come up at interview.) Keep it short, honest and confident. This context and proactive attitude is what separates the shining CVs from the dim ones. Have you ever seen a gap explained really well, or really badly? 👇 #CVTips #CareerBreak #ContractWork #Recruitment #JobSearch … more

posts.text: When a new responsibility emerges, external recruitment often becomes the first option. But it's worth asking another question: Does someone on the existing team already have the foundation to take it on? An employee may have developed relevant skills through a previous project. Another may be ready for greater responsibility but hasn't had the opportunity to demonstrate it. Internal talent won't fill every vacancy. Some roles require specialist expertise or experience the organization doesn't currently have. Still, overlooking existing capabilities can lead to unnecessary recruitment costs and missed development opportunities. Before hiring externally, review the skills already available. Consider employees' experience, interests, demonstrated performance, and readiness to learn. Then identify where training or support could bridge the gap. A stronger workforce strategy considers both the talent you can attract and the talent you can develop. … more

posts.text: U.S. Job Cuts Fall to Lowest October Since 2023 U.S. employers announced 43,994 job cuts in October, down 71% from a year earlier and the lowest October total since 2023, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas, Inc. Through the first 10 months of 2026, announced cuts total 617,189, down 44% from the same period last year and the lowest year-to-date figure since 2022. Challenger's figures track employer announcements rather than completed layoffs, making them an early indicator of corporate employment decisions rather than an official measure of job losses. While the national numbers suggest a more stable labor market, the industry breakdown reveals a much more uneven picture, with food companies leading October at 9,677 announced cuts, followed by technology at 5,576 and services at 5,458. Technology still accounts for 28% of all announced cuts this year, while food-industry cuts are up 43%, transportation cuts have increased 188%, and FinTech cuts are up 543%. The national improvement is significant, but it does not mean every industry is experiencing a healthier labor market. That unevenness also extends to hiring, with employers announcing plans to hire 444,692 workers in October, up 57% from a year earlier and the highest October total since at least 2009. However, Amazon and UPS accounted for 400,000 of those planned positions, nearly 90% of the total, and both announcements were for seasonal employment. Just five companies have announced seasonal hiring plans this year compared with 11 last year, while retailers announced 3,692 job cuts in October even as they planned to hire 13,300 workers. The reasons for layoffs are changing as well, with market and economic conditions accounting for 37% of October's announced cuts, compared with just 1,265 attributed to artificial intelligence. Economic conditions have now overtaken AI as the leading stated reason for job reductions this year, suggesting that broader economic pressures are becoming more prominent even as overall layoff announcements remain relatively low. Taken together with this week's JOLTS and ADP reports, these findings reinforce the distinction between job security and job opportunity, but I think the industry differences deserve more attention. The national labor market can look healthier while workers in industries experiencing continued layoffs see little reason for optimism, particularly if they believe finding another comparable job would be difficult. Two households with similar incomes can therefore have very different expectations about their financial futures simply because they work in different industries, and those expectations can influence spending decisions long before either household experiences an actual loss of income. For Havas Edge, understanding where employment is improving and where uncertainty persists helps explain why consumer spending behavior can differ so significantly across households. … more

posts.text: Everyone wants a remote job. But apparently, nobody wants the version of remote work that employers are actually offering. We spent some time digging through Reddit's biggest remote-work communities this week, and five frustrations kept coming up: 🤔 JOBS ADVERTISED AS REMOTE THAT AREN'T REALLY REMOTE State restrictions, mandatory travel, office visits and geographic limitations. Apparently, "work from anywhere" still needs some fine print. 🚨 SCAMS EVERYWHERE Fake recruiters, suspicious data-entry jobs and companies that are difficult to verify. Finding a legitimate opportunity shouldn't require detective work. 🔎 ACTUALLY FINDING A DECENT JOB People want to know who's hiring, which skills are in demand and what those jobs pay. Not another vague recommendation to "learn coding." 🙄 HAVING TO JUSTIFY WORKING REMOTELY Some people still don't consider working from home a "real" career, even when you're earning a comfortable salary and doing the same work as someone in an office. 👀 EMPLOYERS TURNING REMOTE WORK INTO A SURVEILLANCE OPERATION Webcam monitoring, productivity tracking and keyboard activity reports. One employee reportedly had to submit 160 webcam photos per day. Seriously. What we see here is that people aren't asking for much. They want legitimate opportunities, honest job descriptions, decent pay and the freedom to actually work remotely without being treated like they're doing something wrong. Is that really so much to ask when it's almost 2027 and the entire planet is just a Slack message away? 🤷‍♂️ It's interesting how many of the biggest complaints aren't really about remote work itself. posts.text: One thing I wish more people understood about remote work is that wanting a remote job and being prepared for one are two different things. I get messages from people asking me to give them a remote job. I understand the urgency, and I know many people genuinely need the opportunity. But remote jobs aren’t handed out simply because you ask for them. You need relevant skills, practical knowledge, confidence using digital tools, a good understanding of the role you’re applying for, and the ability to communicate your value to an employer. That’s why learning matters. You don’t need to know everything before you begin, but you do need to be willing to learn, practice, improve, and put yourself out there. posts.text: Remote Work Is a Skillset Too… Being good at your technical job does not automatically mean you are good at remote work. Remote teams often depend heavily on: • Written communication • Time management • Self-management • Documentation • Digital collaboration • Follow-through • Clear updates • Meeting etiquette • Asking for help early • Managing priorities Imagine your manager asks: “What did you complete today?” A strong remote worker can give a concise update: DONE: • Reconciled 24 customer records • Replied to outstanding enquiries • Updated CRM NEXT: • Follow up with 6 customers • Prepare Friday report BLOCKED: • Waiting for access to the billing dashboard That is remote professionalism. You are making your work visible without someone standing beside you. Remote readiness is not just “I can work from home.” It is the ability to communicate, organise and deliver without constant supervision. Start sending yourself daily DONE / NEXT / BLOCKED updates for one week. You are practising a remote-work habit before you even get the job. #RemoteJobs #RemoteWork #JobSearch #CareerTips #JobSeekers #WorkFromHome #RemoteCareer #6000RemoteJobSeekers … more

posts.text: Remote experience is useful, but it isn’t the only way to demonstrate remote-work readiness. Candidates can build credible proof by showing how they communicate, organize tasks, use workplace tools, solve problems, and work independently. A simple portfolio might include: • A professional email • A mock project tracker • A customer-support response • A short screen-recorded process walkthrough Examples from retail, school, volunteering, caregiving, freelancing, and personal projects can also support your case. Describe the situation, your actions, and the result. Add metrics only when they’re accurate. Finally, tailor that proof to the posting. Look for repeated requirements such as written communication, customer service, spreadsheets, scheduling, data entry, troubleshooting, CRM systems, or ticketing tools. Don’t overclaim remote experience. Show that you already have the habits and transferable skills needed to succeed. [link hidden] … more

posts.text: THE REMOTE JOB HUNT IS NOT FOR THE FAINT-HEARTED! 😩💻 Let's talk about the reality of searching for a remote job. You update your CV. You polish your LinkedIn profile. The remote job market is competitive, but giving up guarantees that you won't discover what the next application could bring. Keep learning. Keep improving. Keep applying. Keep showing up. One rejection should not cancel your dreams. One unanswered application should not make you question your worth. posts.text: Remote work is not as remote as people think Remote work, but with restrictions Remote work is supposed to remove geographical barriers. So why does location still determine who gets an opportunity? Companies advertise global opportunities. They talk about hiring the best talent, building diverse teams, and giving people the freedom to work from anywhere. Then you open the application. United States only. Europe only. Selected countries only. Sometimes, the position is described as fully remote, but the opportunity is geographically restricted. I understand that employment regulations, tax arrangements, time zones, and payment infrastructure can create legitimate limitations. But there’s a difference between having operational restrictions and overlooking capable professionals simply because they live elsewhere. Talent isn’t concentrated in a handful of countries. Neither is ambition. If companies genuinely want to access global talent, perhaps they should explore more ways to make international collaboration possible. What does remote work actually mean if your location determines whether you’re allowed to apply? #RemoteWork #GlobalTalent #Hiring #FutureOfWork … more

posts.text: We’re approaching 2027, and some technology companies are STILL insisting that employees show up to the office. I have two female friends whose jobs are very similar to mine. Their work requires nothing more than a laptop, a Wi-Fi connection, and a reliable internet connection to operate. Yet, their companies require them to be in the office at least 3 days a week. Both are mothers. So, their mornings look something like this: • Get the kids ready. • Drop them off at daycare. • Commute to the office. • Spend the day doing a job they could have done from anywhere. • Repeat. The result? At least 15% of their salaries goes towards childcare, not to mention commuting costs, commuting time, and the additional pressure on their daily lives. And every time I think about this, I find myself wondering: How are some of the biggest technology companies still operating with such outdated mindsets? We’re talking about companies that build the future of technology but seem reluctant to embrace one of the simplest ways technology can improve the present: remote work. Flexibility isn’t a luxury. Remote work isn’t a perk. And being physically present in an office doesn’t automatically make someone more productive. Whenever someone asks me why I always work from home, my answer is: Because I’m not a cardio surgeon. 😂 If the job can be done just as effectively with a laptop and Wi-Fi, maybe it’s time to rethink what actually requires an office presence. … more

posts.text: Can we please stop giving remote-work bashers more ammunition? I keep seeing posts from people working from home focusing on the downsides, like getting distracted by housework or all the jobs that need doing around the house. Remote working gets enough of a bad rap without people fortunate enough to have that flexibility adding to it! Some of the comments are unbelievable. People openly admitting they’re watching TV instead of working. Of course, it happens sometimes, but actually putting that in writing on LinkedIn? Really?! And we wonder why some employers want people back in the office! Apparently, everyone's either laying on a beach or doing yoga on a cliff. 😂 The reality is, most normal hard working people are just getting on with their jobs at home. Everyone works differently. When I worked for a company I had a dedicated office and stuck to office hours. You’re not worrying about getting home in time for after-school club (or doggy day care) pick-up or missing the train. Yes, people can go for a walk at lunchtime and probably have more coffee breaks than they would in an office. So what?! I’m a huge advocate for remote working because I know how productive it made me without the noise and distractions of a busy office or the stress of a commute. It’s about getting the job done, not where you do it. Let’s show employers that flexibility and productivity can go hand in hand. … more

posts.text: When I first started working remotely, I thought one of the best parts would be being more comfortable, more relaxed, more in “home mode.” But from day one, I decided to do something differently: Get dressed like I was going to the office. Just wearing something I would normally choose if I were actually heading out to work. And personally, it ended up becoming one of the best productivity habits I’ve had. Not because clothes somehow make you work better. But because they create a small mental separation. When I get dressed for work, it feels like the day actually starts. I stop feeling like I’m just at home with a laptop open, and I shift into work mode. After all this time working remotely, it’s still something I keep doing. It’s simple, but for me, it makes a real difference. … more

posts.text: Candidates, please stop making this mistake. We ask a candidate: “What is your current salary?” They tell us their number, then immediately say: “I know it’s high, and I don’t mind taking less.” Wait… why? How did you decide that your salary is high before even knowing the salary range for the new role? In many cases, the range offered by the employer is actually higher than what the candidate is currently earning. Don’t negotiate against yourself. First, understand the role, responsibilities, market value, and the employer’s salary range. Then have a conversation about compensation. You might be willing to take less for the right opportunity, and that’s completely fine. But don’t offer to lower your salary before anyone even asks you to. Know your value. Ask questions. posts.text: I operate a job channel in Jamaica with over 11,000 followers/job seekers subscribed. My number one rule? I post jobs that disclose the salary or salary range. Simple, right? Well, apparently not. One thing I've noticed is that these jobs are usually government vacancies. When it comes to private-sector companies, very few seem willing to disclose what the position actually pays. And it got me thinking: WHY? Why are we asking people to submit applications, update their CVs, prepare for interviews, spend money on transportation and invest their time, only for them to get through the recruitment process and discover that the salary isn't even remotely aligned with their expectations? Wouldn't it be easier for everyone if employers simply stated what they were prepared to pay from the beginning? I understand that there may be different considerations, experience levels and salary negotiations. But surely, a salary range isn't too much to ask? Job seekers deserve to make informed decisions too. Your time has value. Your qualifications have value. And knowing whether a job can meet your financial expectations before applying should not be considered unreasonable. So, I'm genuinely curious: Why are so many private-sector companies in Jamaica reluctant to disclose salaries in their job advertisements? posts.text: Since 1935, federal law has protected most private-sector employees' right to discuss their pay. And about half of American workers still say their employer prohibits or discourages it. So most people never learn how to bring it up. Here’s a playbook. 1. Start with your own number. In most private-sector jobs, you can share your own pay. Nobody has to share theirs. 2. Ask for the range, not the salary. “Do you know the range for this role?” In Massachusetts, employers with 25 or more employees have to give you the range for your own position when you ask. 3. Compare roles, not people. “What’s a fair range for a Senior Accountant at a company like ours?” It’s easier to answer, and it gets you the same information. 4. Ask before the offer, not after. 17% of applicants who saw a posted range were later offered below it (Patriot Software, 2026). Ask where in the range the offer lands, and why. 5. Then actually ask. The worst answer is no. The best answer is more money. Most people never find out which one they would have gotten. Talking about pay isn’t gossip. It’s information. posts.text: GTK #6 💡 Find out what the research reveals: Researchers analyzed 10 million job postings and conducted one field experiment and two lab experiments to investigate how salary ranges influence job applications and negotiations. They found that women were more likely than men to prefer jobs with narrow salary ranges rather than wide ones. For example: - Narrow salary range: 55.000€ – 75.000€ - Wide salary range: 40.000€ – 90.000€ They were therefore also less likely to negotiate, and ultimately asked for lower salaries. In other words, the width of salary ranges in job postings can unintentionally disadvantage women. But there is a simple way to prevent this effect. When recruiters explained the typical starting salary and how the final salary would be determined: For example: “The typical starting salary is around €65,000. Your exact salary offer will reflect your relevant experience, skill level, and the responsibilities of the role, in line with our standardized compensation guidelines.” - Women's preference for jobs with wide salary ranges increased from 48.5% to 60.3%, reaching the same level as men's. - The difference between men and women in salary negotiations also disappeared. 🤨 Why? - Wide salary ranges create uncertainty about what candidates can realistically expect to earn. - Women are generally more risk-averse than men, making wide salary ranges less attractive to them. - Explaining the typical starting salary and how pay is determined reduces that uncertainty, making wider salary ranges more appealing. 👇 What can recruiters do? Don't just disclose salary ranges. Explain them. When posting a job, specify: - The typical starting salary for candidates meeting the core requirements. - How experience, skills and responsibilities influence the final salary offer. A Junior Frontend Developer and a Senior Frontend Engineer shouldn't automatically have the same salary expectations. 🧮 4. Know your own range. Have a realistic minimum and target figure in mind before the interview. 🤝 5. Be prepared to negotiate. Your answer should communicate flexibility without making it seem like you haven't considered your value. One way to approach the question is: "Based on my understanding of the role, its responsibilities, and the market range, I have a compensation range in mind. However, I'm open to discussing the budget allocated for the position and the overall benefits." posts.text: Who sees your pay ranges first: the candidate who applied yesterday, or the employee who's been with you for three years? Most companies are getting this wrong. In Pave's 2027 report, 80.2% of companies post a salary range on every US job ad. But inside those same companies: - Only 13.9% make an employee's own range automatically available. 43.4% share it on request. 20.5% don't share it at all. So at most companies, a candidate can read a version of the range before an employee can see theirs without asking. I understand how we got here. Candidate transparency arrived through legislation. Conversely, employee transparency is a choice, and most companies haven't really made it yet. But your employees read your job ads too. (and I see this hurt companies all the time) If the ad is the first place someone sees their band, you've lost the chance to explain it. (And "on request" asks people to put their hand up about their own pay, which many may not do.) How I'd give employees at least the same experience as candidates: → Put each person's band in your HRIS, plus the level above → Explain how the bands were built and where you target in the market → Define what each position in the range means → Brief managers before it goes live Your employees should never know less about pay than the people you're trying to hire. Employers who couldn't answer "what does this role pay?" were already losing candidates before the law came in. This is not legal advice. posts.text: In 11 months, I negotiated $71K to $153K as a data analyst in tech My secret is shutting your mouth and not saying any numbers. I never would’ve thought I was worth $140K-153K, so I probably wouldn’t have asked for that much… but multiple companies willingly offered it to me! I realized that saying a number first was me doing their job for them. I was basically telling them exactly how little they could pay me without negotiating. And this way, I was definitely going to lowball myself. Because their budget is almost always more than you think it is. So I stopped saying numbers. Every time a recruiter asked "what are your salary expectations?" I'd say: "I'd love to meet with more members of the team and better understand the role so I can assess the market value. But if you have a budget, I wouldn't mind hearing it.” Then SIT IN THE SILENCE. Don’t fill the awkwardness. Just wait for them to talk. Silence is your power, own it. Companies will almost tell you their budget and if they don’t thats a red flag. Once they named their number, I either said yes, I'm aligned with that range or I moved on. Good negotiation skills literally make you money over time not just in your salary but in your %-based bonuses and raises, 401K contributions, and compounding interest 💅🏻 … more

posts.text: A posted pay range sets expectations before your recruiter says a word. Ogletree's update on New Jersey's proposed pay-transparency rules is a useful prompt to review the posting itself. The regulatory changes discussed are proposals; the state's pay and benefits disclosure law is already in effect. From the candidate's side, the range helps answer a basic question: is this opportunity worth pursuing? If the conversation later reveals a much narrower budget or different compensation, the candidate has to reassess after investing time in the process. The article's employer questions make a useful checklist: - Does the posting show clear minimum and maximum pay? - Are benefits and other compensation described? - Do recruiter and job-board versions provide consistent information? - Can applicants reach linked disclosures without unnecessary hurdles? - Are current employees hearing about promotional opportunities? I would add a question for the recruiter and hiring manager: what would place someone at different points in the range, and does the approved hiring budget support that explanation (and the range)? A broad salary band can encompass progression over a career. The job posting needs to help candidates understand this particular opening. Before publishing, read it as a candidate. Can you understand the pay opportunity, the total package and what still needs clarification before agreeing to an interview? #Compensation #PayTransparency … more

posts.text: I think we need to have a conversation about salary expectations because, what exactly are we doing? 😭😂 You see a job advert. The salary range is clearly stated. You read it, apply, and get shortlisted. Then I call for a quick conversation before scheduling your interview, just to confirm that you're comfortable with the stated range. Suddenly, the salary is no longer okay. 😭 Now we're negotiating. We're explaining. We're going back and forth. But wait… wasn't the salary right there in the advert? 👀 Please, if the salary doesn't work for you, that's completely fine. You have every right to decline an opportunity. Maybe you're worth more. Maybe you have different expectations. No hard feelings. But applying for a role when the advertised salary is already outside your expectations, only to raise the issue when the recruitment process begins, wastes everyone's time. And honestly, recruitment already has enough delays. 😂 Of course, there's nothing wrong with negotiating when there's room to do so. But let's not confuse negotiation with applying for an opportunity you already know doesn't align with your expectations. So candidates, please read the advert before applying. If the salary range, role, or conditions don't align with what you're looking for, it's okay to move on. Reading the advert is the first interview. ❤️ … more

posts.text: 💫Pay transparency isn't just about compliance💫 Most employers say they want to pay people fairly. Fewer are fully confident that their own pay arrangements would hold up if someone looked closely.⬇️ Over time, organisations change. Roles grow, businesses merge and salaries get agreed in very different markets. Each decision might have made sense at the time. Taken together, they can be hard to explain. The EU Pay Transparency Directive and the government's recent consultation on equal pay are bringing this into the open. Our autumn Reward Management Survey suggests it's already changing how organisations think about pay, with an increased push for transparency. Why is one role paid more than another? Why are two people doing similar jobs on different salaries? What determines whether someone progresses to the next pay grade? These aren't unreasonable questions. Employees are already asking the questions. Why is my role paid less than that one? Why are two of us doing similar work on different salaries? Publishing pay ranges won't answer those questions by itself. You need a clear, consistent basis for how jobs are valued and that's what job evaluation gives you. It isn't the most exciting topic on the HR agenda but I would argue it's one of the most important right now. You don't have to fix everything at once. A good start is asking: could our managers explain how someone's pay was decided? 📰Read the full blog here: [link hidden] 💭If an employee asked why they're paid what they are, how confident would you be in your answer? #PayTransparency #PayEquity #JobEvaluation #Reward #HRInsights #EqualPay #RewardManagement #PeopleStrategy … more

posts.text: A headhunter ended our conversation after just 30 seconds. I was still a young woman at the time, working in an office when I received a call from a headhunter’s secretary. They were looking for someone to take on a Branch Manager position at a temporary staffing company specialising in IT. We arranged a phone conversation for 11:00 a.m. The headhunter was supposed to call me. At 11:05 a.m., I still hadn’t heard from him. So I decided to call him myself. He sounded annoyed: “I would have called you.” He was an older gentleman, very direct, factual and straight to the point. Then, without any introduction, he asked: “What are your salary expectations?” I wasn’t prepared for that question. I hesitated for a moment and eventually said €50,000 ??! gross per year. And honestly, I was thinking to myself: I hope that’s not too much! 😬 His response came immediately: “Thank you. This conversation is over.” And he hung up. I was completely stunned. My first thought was: What an idiot! But then I started researching the position and eventually found the original job advertisement on his website. The advertised salary range was €70,000 to €90,000 per year. And suddenly, I understood. I hadn’t asked for too much. I had asked for far too little. 🤦‍♀️ So… Even when you’re impatient, it’s still better to be patient, wait rather than trying to force results… and coming across as insecure won’t get you the job you want. 😉 #Recruitment #CareerAdvice #Nigeria #RemoteJobs #CareerDevelopment … more

posts.text: Can we just ban job postings without a salary range? Hiding the pay doesn’t protect anyone. It just wastes everyone’s time. Here’s how it usually goes. You apply. You do the recruiter screen. Then the hiring manager round, the technical round, the team round. Weeks go by. And at the very end, you finally learn the number, and it’s less than what you make right now. Five rounds, for a role that was never going to work. The company loses too. It spent hours of interviewer time on someone who was always going to say no. As an engineer, this is the part that gets me. If you’re building any system, you check the simplest condition first, before you spend time on the expensive steps. Pay is the simplest condition in hiring. One number. And most companies check it last. Some places already require ranges by law, and those postings prove it’s easy to do. Put the range up front, and the only people who apply are the ones it works for. posts.text: I was scrolling through LinkedIn when Netflix casually announced a job paying up to $605,000, and I almost dropped coffee into another tax bracket. Director of Security & Intelligence. SIX HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS. For that kind of money, I expect the candidate to protect the building, interrogate the Wi-Fi, and personally wrestle every hacker into the opening credits. But naturally, Netflix has requirements. An advanced degree in security. Ten plus years of increasing responsibility at a multinational entertainment studio. Prior leadership overseeing studio security. So basically, they’re hiring Batman, but only if Gotham was a subsidiary of Warner Bros. and Bruce Wayne submitted his transcripts. Imagine having 20 years of military intelligence experience, stopping actual threats, protecting world leaders, and being told, “Unfortunately, your background isn’t sufficiently entertainment focused.” Sorry, General. You may have prevented an international crisis, but have you ever secured a trailer for a reality show about people marrying strangers through a wall? And the salary range? $352,000 to $605,000, all in. You can choose salary versus stock options. No bonus. Oh, the sacrifice! How will this poor executive survive without a bonus? Should we start a GoFundMe? I want to see the interview process. Round one: recruiter screening. Round two: panel. Round three: personality assessment. Round four: explain a gap in your resume from 2009. Round five: stop a simulated cyberattack while the hiring manager asks where you see yourself in five years. Round six: a one way video where you describe your greatest weakness to an empty screen. Round seven: protect the CEO from a rogue Netflix recommendation. “Why Netflix?” “Because apparently you’re paying enough for me to buy the entire neighborhood and install a moat.” “Are you comfortable working in a fast paced environment?” “Ma’am, I once evacuated a stadium.” “Yes, but can you handle feedback from a vice president who calls every meeting a sync?” And let’s talk about the title: Security & Intelligence. Will this person finally investigate who keeps canceling shows after one season? Because THAT is the cold case America needs solved. Forget encrypted files. Find the executive who looked at a beloved series and said, “Interesting. Let’s replace it with twelve episodes of influencers arguing beside a pool.” I also hope the role includes tracking down the person who invented Netflix’s “Are you still watching?” message. Yes, Netflix. I’m still watching. It’s Saturday. I’m wearing sweatpants. You have no moral authority here. Of course, the actual work may be serious and the compensation may reflect that. But the job post reads like they want the head of the CIA, a Hollywood producer, and Batman stacked inside one trench coat. My only question: If I get rejected, will Netflix at least turn the experience into a six part documentary called “Overqualified: The Man Who Couldn’t Get Past Workday”? … more

But ask any hiring manager how valuable it is. • Work ethic: Experience means very little if someone needs to be chased every day to get the job done. • Adaptability: Industries change. Technology changes. The people who can learn and adapt are the ones who remain valuable. Here’s the uncomfortable truth. Some businesses would rather leave a $100k position vacant for 6 months than hire someone with 80% of the skills and train the remaining 20%. Then complain there’s a talent shortage. Give someone with the right attitude, transferable skills and genuine ambition proper training and a real opportunity. posts.text: A candidate can like your company, accept the salary range and still turn down your offer because of the medical benefits. That’s why benchmarking your PEO needs to go deeper than the monthly price. Start with these five things: → Network Are their doctors, specialists and hospitals in it? The same insurance carrier can offer different networks. → Coinsurance After meeting the deductible, how much of the bill does the employee still pay? → Maximum out-of-pocket What could an employee or family have to spend in a bad medical year? What falls outside that limit? → Deductible How much do they pay before the plan starts sharing costs, and which services are covered before that? → Premium What do the company and employee each pay every month? Then check prescription coverage, copays and out-of-network benefits. Those details can change the comparison considerably. Imagine saving an employee $100 a month in premiums while increasing their deductible by $3,000. You’ve lowered their fixed cost. You may also have increased what they’ll spend when they need care. Understand where the savings come from. And remember who has to live with the decision. A candidate whose specialist isn’t in the network or whose child’s medication isn’t covered may choose another employer. Your existing employees are making those comparisons too. At Dinsmore Steele®, we compare the medical offerings alongside the costs so you can see what you’re gaining, what you’re giving up and whether the trade makes sense. A cheaper PEO isn’t a better deal if the savings make your job offers harder to accept. posts.text: If you are a foreigner applying for jobs in Singapore and the replies stop after the first message, or you keep wondering whether your nationality is the problem, this is worth reading. I review CVs from professionals applying to Singapore from abroad as well as from people who have just relocated, and the same few gaps keep turning up. In most of them, the issue was not the experience or the passport. It was positioning: nothing on the page told the employer that hiring this person was a practical option. Three things I keep finding: 1️⃣ The role cannot pay enough for a work pass. The Employment Pass has a minimum monthly salary that rises with age, starting from $5,600 now and from $6,000 for new applications from 1 January 2027. If the advertised range tops out below the minimum for your age, the employer cannot hire you on that pass, however strong your CV is. 2️⃣ Page one does not say where you are or when you can start. A common version: a strong CV with no location, no notice period and no mention of Singapore. The employer has to guess how soon you could join, so they move on to someone they do not have to guess about. 3️⃣ Employers are described only for a home-country reader. “Regional Manager at [company]” means little to a hiring manager here who has never heard of it. One line on markets, headcount or scale fixes that. What works better: • Check the salary range against the pass minimum for your age before you apply • Put “Relocating to Singapore, available from [month]”, or your current pass status, under your name • Add one line of scale to every employer you list If you are applying to Singapore from abroad and want to know what an employer here sees first on your CV, send it over and I will tell you. … more

The deadline for EU countries to introduce these rules was June 7, 2026. However, several countries are still working on implementing them. Germany has not yet completed the implementation, while countries such as Italy have already introduced new legislation. posts.text: Pay transparency compliance is failing the same way DEI reporting failed before it. The data was never built to answer the question now being asked of it. A pay range disclosure law does not ask what someone was paid. A pay range disclosure law asks whether that pay sits inside a defensible range for a given job, level, and location. Most HR data stacks cannot answer that question today, and the reason is not pay. The reason is job level. Payroll, HRIS, and compensation systems each code job level differently, for their own purpose, and each code is correct inside its own system. None of the three matches what a pay equity analysis means by comparable work. posts.text: It's a live debate right now, not a hypothetical one. The UK government is currently consulting on requiring employers to publish pay information in job adverts, with that consultation closing 27 October. The proposal on the table is narrower than people sometimes assume — pay and conditions information in job adverts, or before interview if there isn't one, rather than the broader pay-equity rules some EU countries have introduced. The detail that matters most — how wide a pay range is allowed to be — has deliberately been left to future regulation. You don't need to wait for legislation to make this decision. Around 21.6% of UK employers already publish pay information in their adverts voluntarily — meaning most still don't, but a meaningful minority have already concluded it's worth doing regardless of what the law eventually requires. From where I sit, hiding the number rarely protects an employer — it just means you find out a candidate's expectations don't match yours at offer stage, several interview rounds too late. Publishing a realistic range filters out mismatched applications before they start. The genuine concern isn't transparency itself — it's publishing a range before you're confident it's the right one, and then finding it hard to move off it later. posts.text: If you ask for my current salary, share your budget first. In almost every interview or LinkedIn message, HR asks: "What's your current salary?" But when the candidate asks: "What's the budget for this role?", the answer is usually: "We'll discuss it later" or "It depends on your experience." Let's be honest. Every company already has an approved salary range for the position before they even post the job. The budget exists. It's not a secret to them, only to the candidate. So why does the current salary matter? Too often, it's used as an anchor. Instead of paying what the role is worth, the offer is based on what the person earned before, usually just above their current package and close to the minimum of the range. That's not fair, for a few reasons: A salary should reflect the role, responsibilities, and value you bring, not your last company's pay scale. Someone who was underpaid before shouldn't stay underpaid forever. Negotiation only works when both sides share information. Right now, one side shows all its cards and the other shows none. My simple suggestion to HR and recruiters: Share the salary range early, ideally in the job post or the first call. If you ask for the candidate's current salary, be ready to share your budget too. Make offers based on the role and the candidate's skills, not their salary history. Transparency builds trust. Candidates who feel respected during hiring become employees who stay. My suggestion for all candidates: it's okay to politely ask, "Could you share the budgeted range for this role?" You deserve to know. What do you think? posts.text: So I made a comment on a post about pay transparency, and boy oh boy did a lot of people have something to say about it. 😂 I'm not sharing the link because I don't need another 50 notifications. But I've been thinking, and I believe I've found an interesting middle ground. Instead of making compensation about what your colleagues earn, what if we made it about what YOU could earn? Here's my proposal: Employees can ask their managers for the FULL salary range of their role. And managers are LEGALLY obligated to provide it, along with an explanation of where the employee sits within that range. ================================ Scenario 1: Top 10% of the salary range Employee: Hey, I'd like to see the pay range for my role, please. Manager: Sure! You're at the 90th percentile. You're approaching the ceiling for this role, so a promotion is probably the best path to a significant increase. Employee: Great! What do I need to do to get promoted? Manager: Let's build a plan with milestones around it. ================================== Scenario 2: Anything below that Employee: Hey, I'd like to see the pay range for my role, please. Manager: Sure! You're currently at the 70th percentile. Employee: Well, I feel I deserve more because of X, Y and Z. Manager: Alright, let's review those points and see whether a compensation adjustment is justified. That's it. No need to know what John from accounting makes. No need to compare yourself with Susan from marketing. Just transparency around your own compensation, where you stand, and what you need to do to earn more. Pay transparency should empower employees to negotiate their worth, not just compare their salaries. What do you think? … more

posts.text: A Question About PF Contributions and Salary Transparency – Something HR Needs to Address! Recently, I came across a salary structure that raised an important concern regarding the treatment of Employee and Employer PF contributions. While Employee PF contributions are deducted from an employee's salary, the Employer PF contribution is the statutory responsibility of the employer. However, in certain salary structures, employees may notice that the employer's PF contribution is also impacting their monthly take-home salary. This raises some important questions: 1. Why is the employer's PF contribution also reducing an employee's take-home salary? 2. If the employer's contribution is a statutory obligation, why is its financial impact being passed on to employees? 3. Are employees clearly informed about this adjustment during salary discussions? 4. Why isn't the distinction between Employee PF and Employer PF contributions explained transparently in the salary breakup? Including the employer's PF contribution in the overall CTC is understandable. However, deducting or adjusting it against an employee's agreed salary is a different matter and deserves proper clarification. Shouldn't employees have complete transparency about every component of their salary and every deduction affecting their monthly take-home pay? I would genuinely appreciate insights from HR leaders, payroll professionals and industry experts on this subject. Transparency in compensation should be a standard practice, not something employees have to investigate themselves. #hr #payroll #epfo #employee #retail #Hrpayroll … more

posts.text: Listened in on a Talent Acquisition roundtable this morning, and heard about a hiring trend that is completely defeating the purpose of pay transparency: Employers weaponizing compensation asks against candidates who ask for a number squarely inside the posted salary range. If you advertise a salary range, but immediately disqualify an applicant the moment they target the upper half of it, you did not post a range in good faith. While employers retain discretion over final offers, using salary requests within an advertised band as a screening gate runs dangerously afoul of both the letter and the spirit of labor statutes: The "Good Faith" Mandate: Pay transparency laws across California (SB 1162 / SB 642), New York State (Labor Law § 194-b), Washington State (RCW 49.58.110), Colorado (Equal Pay for Equal Work Act), and Illinois mandate that employers post a bona fide, good-faith wage scale that the organization genuinely intends and is budgeted to pay at hire. If the top 30% of your band is purely decorative and triggering disqualifications, that posted range is materially misleading and vulnerable to regulatory audit and statutory penalties. Salary History Bans & Screen-Out Protections: Over 22 states and numerous cities (e.g., California Labor Code § 432.3, New York, Illinois) explicitly make it unlawful to screen applicants based on past compensation or refuse to interview/hire based on prior wage metrics. When companies push candidates into compensation corners early to disqualify them, they risk creating pretextual rejections that invite disparate impact scrutiny. Pay Equity & Discrimination Exposure (Title VII / Equal Pay Acts): Weaponizing salary asks often disproportionately impact underrepresented groups. Studies consistently demonstrate that women and marginalized professionals are penalized more harshly during compensation discussions. Posting an inflated band just to attract top-tier talent, only to filter out anyone who takes you at your word is bait-and-switch recruiting. Pay transparency wasn't passed so organizations could check a compliance box while preserving information asymmetry. It was passed to create level, transparent negotiations. Candidate screening should be about competence, impact, and culture add: not a guessing game where naming an approved number disqualifies you. Let's do better! #PayTransparency #HiringEthics #Recruiting #EqualPay #HumanResources #TalentAcquisition … more

posts.text: Can we have an honest conversation about the cost of looking for a job? One thing we rarely discuss when encouraging people to look for work is that job hunting itself requires financial resources. Let's take Upwork, for example. You need Connects to submit proposals for most opportunities. Sometimes you spend money applying for several jobs without getting a single response. Add reliable internet, electricity, a laptop, subscriptions and other resources needed to remain competitive. Essentially, you need money to pursue an opportunity that might eventually help you make money. And let's not forget the emotional cost of constantly applying, following up, attending interviews and sometimes being ghosted. We need to acknowledge that not everyone looking for employment is financially comfortable. Some people are unemployed, struggling to meet basic needs, yet are expected to keep investing in their job search. Now, on to another issue: salary transparency. Why advertise a job vacancy without disclosing the salary or at least providing a salary range? I genuinely believe employers should include compensation details in their job advertisements. Let an adult decide whether the proposed salary is worth their time, skills, experience and effort. If the budget is fixed, state it. If the salary is negotiable depending on experience, communicate that too. Job seekers deserve the opportunity to make informed decisions before investing their time in lengthy application processes and interviews. Transparency saves time for both the employer and the applicant. We cannot keep telling people to value their skills, negotiate better and know their worth while making it unnecessarily difficult for them to understand what an opportunity actually offers. Looking for work is work in itself. And perhaps it's time we started acknowledging that. … more

posts.text: Companies Want Salary Transparency During Hiring, But Not Among Employees! Dear Corporate India, let's talk about another interesting corporate practice. 🤔 During recruitment, the first few questions are usually: What's your current CTC? What's your expected CTC? How much are you willing to negotiate? Do you have any competing offers? Companies want complete transparency when it comes to understanding how much they need to pay you. But when employees discuss their salaries with colleagues? Suddenly, it's considered inappropriate! Why this double standard? Let's understand a few uncomfortable realities: 📌 Same role, different salaries: Two employees with similar qualifications, experience and responsibilities may receive significantly different compensation. 📌 Salary confidentiality: Employees are often discouraged from discussing their compensation with colleagues. 📌 Unequal negotiation power: Employees who negotiate aggressively during recruitment may secure better packages than those who don't. 📌 Existing employees vs new hires: Sometimes, a newly hired employee earns more than someone who has been contributing to the organisation for years. 📌 Lack of transparency: Employees often have no clear understanding of how salary structures, increments and compensation bands work. Now, let's be fair. Not every salary difference is discrimination. Experience, performance, specialised skills, responsibilities and market conditions can justify differences. But shouldn't employees at least have some clarity about how compensation decisions are made? If two employees perform similar roles, shouldn't there be a transparent and reasonable basis for their compensation differences? Companies cannot expect employees to negotiate confidently during recruitment while discouraging conversations that help them understand their market value. And here's something worth thinking about: Salary secrecy doesn't automatically create salary fairness. Transparency can help employees identify inequalities and encourage organisations to address them. 💬 Let's discuss: Do you think employees should openly discuss their salaries with colleagues, or should compensation remain confidential? I'd love to hear different perspectives. #SalaryTransparency #CorporateIndia #SalaryNegotiation #PayEquity #CorporateCulture #EmployeeRights #HRPractices #WorkplaceEquality #CareerGrowth … more

posts.text: Pay transparency is putting more pressure on the quality of compensation decisions. Once employees can see the range, they naturally begin asking harder questions about how decisions are made within it. Why am I positioned here? What would change that position? How are exceptions handled? Would another leader make the same call? Those questions are useful because they reveal whether the organization has real clarity behind its compensation practices. A published range can create visibility. It cannot create consistency, explain progression, define manager judgment, or establish the principles behind an individual pay decision. That is why I think the next phase of pay transparency will be less about disclosure and more about decision quality. posts.text: "Competitive salary" may be on borrowed time. In last week's Budget, the Chancellor said he'd heard the calls for salary ranges in job adverts. posts.text: I genuinely think this is a good idea. Many years ago, when I was less "secure" in my work, I wasted an insane amount of time interviewing for jobs with unrealistic salary ranges. Now, I won't even take a second glance at a role or recruiter message if there isn't a clearly defined number listed. And yes, I will also mock the ones where the numbers are stupidly low as well. But in reality, most people don't have that luxury. Candidates apply for roles with no idea if it will pay what they want. They apply for roles where they get an offer, then get lowballed on the salary because they have no idea what the company was willing to pay. They think they can "negotiate" a good deal, but they dont have enough information to know what they are negotiating against. Then they take the role and don't realise the company is paying more for other people it hires for the same job. There is no benefit to the candidate here. Even the few who think they won the negotiation didn't. They just got close to the upper band the company was willing to pay. What makes it more frustrating is that the overwhelming evidence shows that women and minority groups get statistically lower offers, so they are "negotiating" from a much worse position. Forcing adverts to include salary information (range, fixed number, whatever) helps to minimise this. It isn't perfect, but it is better. Dont let perfection become the enemy of good, or nothing ever changes. Showing a salary is an improvement. Dont let recruiters and hiring managers convince you otherwise. … more

posts.text: Pay transparency is becoming a bigger part of how employers recruit in Europe, and I wanted to understand what it means for Ireland. The EU Pay Transparency Directive set a deadline of 7 June 2026 for member states to bring it into national law. Ireland did not meet that deadline. Progress is now being made. On 21 October 2026, the Employment Equality and Institutional Burials (Amendment) Bill 2026 passed both Houses of the Oireachtas. It was due to go to the President for consideration, and I couldn't find a commencement date. What I took from it: • Employers with 50 or more employees will report their gender pay gap information through a central Gender Pay Gap Portal. • The public will be able to view and compare employers and sectors. • The Directive also requires employers to share salary ranges with candidates and bans questions about pay history. From what I found, these recruitment rules are not yet law in Ireland. As a first-year HRM student, I'm interested in how this will affect job advertising, pay structures and employer branding. posts.text: 15 interviews. 8 leading companies. 4 months. The past four months have given me a new perspective on Finland’s engineering job market. Following my time at GE HealthCare, I began exploring opportunities in electronics manufacturing, test engineering, automation, and quality engineering. What followed was approximately 15 interviews across 8 well-established companies operating in Finland. When I shared these numbers with a few friends, some were genuinely surprised. I hadn’t thought much about the numbers myself. I was simply focused on the next opportunity. The journey included technical assessments, multiple interview rounds, discussions with hiring managers, some disappointments, and a few job offers. Not every offer aligned with my salary expectations or career goals, which taught me something important: Finding a job and finding the right job are two different things. One topic that stood out was salary transparency. Going through several interview rounds only to discover that compensation expectations differ significantly can be frustrating for both candidates and employers. That’s why I welcome the EU Pay Transparency Directive and the conversation around making salary information available earlier in recruitment. Personally, I believe salary ranges in job advertisements would help both sides make more informed decisions. Beyond that, this experience made me appreciate how much goes into a job search that we rarely talk about. We often celebrate the final outcome, but behind it are countless hours of preparation, uncertainty, difficult decisions, and personal growth. I’m particularly grateful to the recruiters, hiring managers, career coaches, and friends who offered their time, encouragement, and feedback along the way. I also recognize that many talented professionals in Finland are facing much tougher circumstances. My experience is just one perspective, not a reflection of everyone’s reality. I’ve gathered dozens of practical lessons throughout this journey and hope to share some in future posts, while respecting the confidentiality of recruitment processes. A few questions worth discussing: • Should salary ranges be included in all job advertisements? • How can employers provide more constructive feedback to candidates? • Beyond salary, what makes an opportunity worth accepting or declining? Transparency and confidentiality don’t have to be mutually exclusive. We often talk about where people end up. Perhaps we should talk a little more about what happens along the way. #Finland #JobMarket #Engineering #Recruitment #SalaryTransparency … more

posts.text: In case you missed it… Last week the EHRC called to an end of salary secrecy! The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) released a clear set of recommendations calling for an overhaul of the UK equal pay framework. Among them: giving workers the right to request salary details for colleagues performing similar work and officially banning salary history queries during recruitment. It mirrors the direction of travel we are seeing with the EU Pay Transparency Directive, and it highlights how quickly administrative pay secrecy is collapsing globally. Historically, many reward models relied heavily on opacity. Using a candidate's prior salary as the baseline for a new offer simply anchored legacy disparities into new compensation structures. At Amazon, we have had a global ban on requesting prior salary details for a number of years. In practice, removing that metric forces hiring mechanisms to focus strictly on objective job pricing, internal equity, and the candidate’s actual capability rather than historical negotiation leverage. Waiting for legislation to force change is usually a sign of reactive governance. When you proactively eliminate salary history queries and build clear, objective range architectures, the operational benefits are immediate: - Offer acceptance and candidate trust increase because roles are priced on internal value, not historical pay. - Internal mobility becomes far cleaner as employees understand the exact capability thresholds required for progression. - Pay compression and equity risks are caught and resolved before they turn into systemic liabilities. Pay transparency is shifting from a compliance obligation to a core operational trust mechanism. posts.text: Pay transparency laws in 2026 now require you to defend every salary on your books, not just job postings. The shift matters. Job-ad transparency is table stakes. Internal pay structure transparency is different. A regulator or employee can now ask why Person A in the same role makes 18% more than Person B, and "that's what we hired them at" doesn't close the gap. The compression risk Neil Vicente flagged in Thomson Reuters' latest Payroll Pulse is real. You don't have to pay everyone the same. You do have to articulate why the differences exist. Experience gap. Promotion timing. Scope creep in the role. Market adjustment when you hired. Performance differential tied to documented outcomes. Those hold up. Gut feel doesn't. For founders and HR-of-one operators running 25 to 500 people, this means an audit before the question arrives. Pull your current roster. Map title to comp. Ask yourself: could I explain this to a lawyer? If the answer is no, you have a comp debt problem that's no longer theoretical. This isn't about compression for its own sake. It's about having a system that survives scrutiny. The companies getting ahead aren't the ones paying everyone equally. They're the ones who can document the logic. What's your current comp structure based on? Title, tenure, market data, performance, or some combination nobody wrote down? #paytransparency #compensation #peopleops #compliance … more

posts.text: Have you ever heard one of these phrases at the dinner table, at work or in the comments? Save this post, here’s how to respond next time. “It’s because women work fewer hours.” Our figure measures the hourly pay gap: it compares one hour of a woman’s work with one hour of a man’s. So even if everyone worked full-time, the gap would still exist. “It’s because they look after the children.” Exactly: the gap widens after the birth of the first child, as Nobel Prize-winning economist Claudia Goldin has shown, for mothers but not fathers. It’s not that women’s work is worth less; it’s that the burden of care is still unequally distributed. Nearly 30% of employed women work part-time, compared with 8% of men, and a third of them do so involuntarily (INSEE). “They just need to negotiate.” You can only negotiate effectively when you have the information. Without pay transparency, women don’t know the salary range for a position or how much their colleagues earn. This is precisely what the European Pay Transparency Directive is designed to change. “That’s not true. Give me an example.” Here’s one: 87% of nursing staff are women, with an average gross monthly salary of around €2,500, while 72% of police officers are men, earning around €3,300. And when teaching was a predominantly male profession, teachers’ average salary was close to the median wage. It has since fallen to around 75% of it. “The gap is only 4% for the same job.” That 4% represents the share of the pay gap that cannot be explained by anything other than gender. The 11.8% figure reflects the actual inequality: fewer promotions, fewer well-paid positions and lower wages in female-dominated professions. See you on #19Novembre10h51 … more

posts.text: “Competitive salary” isn’t a salary. Put the range in the job advert. Three interview rounds is too long to wait to hear the number. By the time pay comes up, a candidate may have taken time off work, paid for transport across Lagos twice, prepared a case study and sat through a panel. Then the offer comes in below what they earn now, and everyone has lost a month. Employers lose too. The role goes back to market after the final round, and the candidates with the most options often skip adverts that don’t say what the job pays. The usual objections don’t hold up well. “It weakens our negotiating position.” A range still leaves room to negotiate. It just starts the conversation in the right place. “Our current staff will see it.” If your team would be upset to see what a new hire could earn, the advert didn’t create that problem. It only made it visible. “Everyone will ask for the top of the range.” Some will. That’s what the interviews are for. Parts of Europe are making it law. The EU Pay Transparency Directive requires employers to give candidates the starting pay or range, in the advert or before the first interview, and stops them asking about pay history. Countries were due to adopt it by June 2026, and only four had fully done so by the deadline, so even there it’s moving slowly. We don’t need a directive to start. If you’re hiring, put the range in the advert. You’ll probably get fewer applications, and more of the right ones. If you’re applying, ask for the range on the first call. A company that won’t share it before round three has already told you something. … more

posts.text: Want to know what your colleagues earn? You might soon have the right to find out. 👀 And I think greater pay transparency could be a VERY good thing. The Equality and Human Rights Commission has recommended giving employees a legal right to request relevant pay information where they suspect pay discrimination. It's also calling for employers to publish salaries on job adverts AND stop asking candidates about their previous salary. YES. 👏 Because I've never understood why what somebody earned in their LAST job should determine what they're worth in their NEXT one. Imagine two candidates applying for exactly the same role. Same level of experience. Same skills. Responsibilities. But one is earning £45k and the other £55k. Why should that mean one gets offered less? Especially when we know women's careers are more likely to have been interrupted by maternity leave, caring responsibilities, career breaks or periods of part-time work. If you've been historically underpaid, basing your next salary on your previous one can simply carry that disadvantage from job to job. And secrecy doesn't exactly help. People can work alongside each other for YEARS doing comparable jobs without knowing there's a significant difference in what they're being paid. You can't question a pay gap you don't know exists. Of course, this doesn't mean everyone doing a similar job must automatically earn exactly the same amount. There can be legitimate reasons for differences in pay - experience, responsibilities, performance, location and other factors. But employers should be able to EXPLAIN those differences. That's the bit I think matters. Pay people based on the role they're doing, the skills and experience they bring and the value of the job. Not what another employer decided they were worth five years ago. And if your pay structures are fair and defensible? Transparency shouldn't be something to fear. 💗 … more

The right to information on individual pay and average pay by gender. 👉 How to prepare Start with your data: check it, clean it, fix it. Design the process, the flow and the communication before the first question lands. Fair pay by design. 👉 What if you can't pay the most? Go back to basics. Have a clear EVP that is aligned with your culture and business needs, and is actually true. Make learning tangible: a set amount, access to tools, an internal academy. Give people real career paths and grow managers from within. Build employee advocacy and referrals. Offer flexible benefits. One risk was named honestly: legislation can put us in boxes.
