posts.text: Your employer's PF contribution should not come at the cost of your take-home salary. A change in PF policy should strengthen employees' financial security — not silently reduce their monthly earnings. Following the revision of the EPF wage ceiling, many employees are seeing changes in their salary structures. But an important question needs to be asked: Can an employer shift its own statutory PF contribution burden onto employees by reducing their wages or salary components? Section 12 of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, specifically restricts employers from reducing employees' wages or employment benefits merely because of their liability to pay PF contributions. Consider what employees are experiencing: - Fixed CTC remains unchanged. - Employer PF contribution is adjusted within the existing CTC. - Salary components such as Special Pay are reduced. - Monthly take-home salary goes down. For employees, this is not just a payroll adjustment. It directly affects monthly household budgets, rent, bills, savings and financial commitments. Retirement savings are important. But employees should not be made to bear the employer's statutory contribution through reduced wages. I believe every employer should provide: 1. A transparent revised CTC structure. 2. A clear explanation of employee and employer PF contributions. 3. Written justification for any reduction in salary components. 4. Confirmation that the restructuring complies with applicable labour laws. A social security reform should protect employees without compromising their present financial stability. Employees deserve transparency, fairness and respect for their hard-earned salaries. #EPF #PF #EmployeeRights #LabourLaws #SalaryStructure #CTC #TakeHomeSalary #India … more

posts.text: 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁, 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗻𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗳𝗶𝗿𝗲𝘀. If you run a business of 15 to 1,000 people, you might wonder why pay transparency is your problem. Not because of fines. Not because of headlines. Because of your people. Do not take my word for it. Take the researchers’. Across 183 studies, people who see their pay as fair are clearly less likely to leave. And people who find the pay process fair trust their employer more (Colquitt et al., 2001). Here is the part most people miss: how you become transparent matters as much as what you show. → Explaining how pay is decided builds trust (SimanTov-Nachlieli & Bamberger, 2021). → Showing who earns what, with no context or explanation, backfires. Below-median staff were 20% more likely to say they were very likely to look for a new job. Being both dissatisfied and likely to look went up by 40% (Card et al., 2012). So the order is: build foundations like job architecture, job levelling and salary bands, and connect them to benchmark data. Calculate the gaps, fix them if they are not justified, and then be transparent. Which would you rather know: what your colleagues earn, or how your own pay was decided? PS: You might not know this about me, but I am a geek at heart. I studied psychology, and my statements and numbers are grounded in peer-reviewed research or own research. posts.text: 5 Things You Can Do to Benefit Your Company AND Job Applicants … I have already posted about the Government proposals to ensure that pay structures are made transparent on job adverts. I included some of the benefits to employers, such as more applicants, and more quality ones at that, and time saving in the recruitment process. You definitely don’t want to end up in an industrial tribunal either – and being transparent about salary can also help close pay gaps across gender, race, disability and other factors. And by the way – it’s going to apply to businesses of any size … So here are some ideas (please add your own I’d be very interested to hear them) as to what you can do to be ready for Government changes and embrace what may be a culture shift for the better: • Obvious one - a salary range is transparent on every job advert. • Update existing job posts so that you are practising and ready. • Give information about other benefits such as bonuses, healthcare, pension contribution, annual leave flexible/hybrid working, geographical location, etc. • Look at Hiring Insights on “Indeed” to see what other employers are offering for similar job titles in the area. This will help you stay competitive. • Don’t advertise a wide salary range spanning more than one grade. Candidates are likely to read this as a single range. When you make them an offer at the bottom of it, they are less likely to accept the job or trust you. If the Government should plan to audit/assess offerings, be ready… Write your salary ranges down, note why you pay what you pay, and keep the records. Your published pay ranges and each advert as published. Record all the places where you published it. Because… They are likely to look at whether you have such a framework and that is has been applied to your vacancies. As the results of the year-long Government discussions on pay transparency become… well… transparent, we will have a clearer picture of the requirements. I feel sure that their new legislation will be rolled out gradually, but ducks in a row and all that! Whether you are a HR professional, Job Seeker, or looking for a Career Transition… If you have any thoughts on what it may look like, or on what else will be best practice, I’d love to hear them. … more

posts.text: Something I've been wondering throughout my job search… I genuinely don't understand the benefit to employers of advertising salary ranges that they have no intention of actually paying. More than half of the positions I've interviewed for recently have had salary ranges that look promising in the job posting, only for the actual budget to be significantly lower once you get into the interview process. And I keep asking myself… how does this benefit the employer? Think about the time involved: - Reviewing applications and selecting candidates. - Scheduling and conducting multiple interviews. - Having candidates prepare for assessments and presentations. - Investing time in getting to know someone, only to discover that you're nowhere near aligned on compensation. Wouldn't it make more sense to be upfront from the beginning? If a company is budgeting $65K–$70K, why advertise $80K–$100K? You're potentially interviewing people who would never have applied if the real salary had been disclosed. I understand that salary ranges can have flexibility depending on experience, but there's a difference between flexibility and advertising a number that isn't realistic. As someone actively navigating the job market, I find it frustrating, but I also genuinely question the business strategy behind it. Isn't transparency supposed to benefit both sides? I'd really love to hear the employer and recruiter perspective on this one. #SalaryTransparency #Recruitment #Hiring #JobSearch #WorkplaceCulture … more

posts.text: Many companies are still taking a wait-and-see approach to the EU Pay Transparency Directive. They want to see the national legislation first, understand the exact obligations, and then decide how to respond. It sounds reasonable. But consider what happens in the meantime. Your compensation structure doesn't become easier to review just because legislation is pending. Your salary data doesn't become more consistent on its own. Historical pay decisions don't suddenly become easier to explain. And getting HR, Finance, and management aligned can take more time than expected. Imagine discovering that: → Different departments use different criteria when setting salaries. → Some employees have salary increases that are difficult to justify objectively. → Job descriptions no longer reflect actual responsibilities. → Compensation information is scattered across spreadsheets, systems, and individual records. → Management has no common approach to explaining pay differences. These situations cannot always be addressed quickly. They require analysis, conversations, documentation, and sometimes difficult decisions. Waiting for national transposition before reviewing them could leave your organization with unnecessary time pressure. 𝗦𝗼, 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝗼 𝗻𝗼𝘄? posts.text: Most pay disparities inside companies don’t happen by malice—they accumulate through years of administrative drift. 📉⚖️ When compensation offers are driven by aggressive candidate negotiations, past salary anchoring, and ad-hoc retention counter-offers, wide pay gaps quietly emerge between colleagues doing the exact same work. The result? Internal distrust, disengaged top talent, and severe legal liability under emerging pay transparency regulations. A truly equitable workplace doesn't rely on assumptions—it runs a Pay Equity Audit: A Practical HR Review of Compensation Gaps: 🔹 The 4 Steps to an Audit-Ready Compensation Structure: 1. Clean the Baseline: Standardize roles by job levels and control for legitimate factors like performance, certifications, and experience. 2. Run Statistical Regressions: Separate the controlled pay gap (equal pay for equal work) from the raw median gap (opportunity and representation gaps). 3. Ring-Fence Remediation Funds: Fix wage gaps through a dedicated equity budget rather than raiding the annual performance merit pool. 4. Fix the Root Causes: Stop asking candidates for past payslips, enforce strict hiring bands, and conduct bi-annual equity checks before appraisal cycles. Fair pay isn't just an ethical standard—it is a core talent retention strategy and an essential pillar of corporate governance. #PayEquity #CompensationAndBenefits #TotalRewards #HRCompliance #PeopleOperations #HRStrategy #PayTransparency #TalentRetention #CHROInsights #MyhrsgPortfolio #myHRSG … more

posts.text: I used to judge candidates who asked about salary before agreeing to attend an interview. Today, I see things differently. When I first started my career in HR, whenever I called a candidate to invite them for an interview and they asked: "Please, before we proceed, may I know the salary range for this position?" I would honestly think, Are you even interested in the job? Why not attend the interview first? Sometimes, I would interpret the question as a lack of seriousness, unwillingness to work or an excessive focus on money. But years down the line, experience has taught me something different. That candidate wasn't necessarily being difficult. They were being practical. Think about it. A candidate may need to: - Take time off their current job to attend an interview. - Spend money on transportation. - Rearrange personal and family commitments. - Prepare for the interview. - Go through multiple stages of recruitment. Only to eventually discover that the salary is nowhere near their expectations. And let's be honest, employers also invest time and resources in the recruitment process. So, why shouldn't salary alignment be discussed early? I've come to understand that asking about compensation doesn't automatically mean a candidate is only interested in money. It could mean they understand their financial responsibilities, know their worth, have done their research and simply want to establish whether the opportunity is mutually beneficial. As HR professionals, we must understand that recruitment is a two-way process. We assess candidates, but candidates are also assessing us. Transparency about compensation is not a favour to candidates. It is part of creating a professional and respectful recruitment experience. One thing I've learnt throughout my HR journey is that experience doesn't just teach you how to do your job better; sometimes, it challenges the very things you once believed. My question to fellow HR professionals and recruiters: When a candidate asks about the salary range before agreeing to an interview, what's your honest reaction? Do you see it as a red flag or a perfectly reasonable question? Let's have an honest conversation. 👇 #HumanResources #Recruitment #TalentAcquisition #HRLessons #CandidateExperience #PeopleManagement #CareerGrowth … more

posts.text: Good morning, everyone. Having spent almost six months actively searching for employment and using LinkedIn on an almost daily basis, there are a few things I have noticed that I believe could make the experience better for job seekers. I am sharing these observations constructively, in the hope that they might encourage some positive changes and benefit others going through the same process. 1. Feedback following job applications This is probably my biggest concern. Over the past six months, I have applied for numerous positions, whether through Easy Apply, company websites or external recruitment platforms. In most cases, I receive an automated email confirming that my application has been submitted. However, what often follows is silence. Whether successful or unsuccessful, applicants deserve some form of feedback. A simple acknowledgement that an application has been reviewed and a decision has been made would make a considerable difference. 2. Salary transparency I have noticed that while some employers include salary details or a pay range in their advertisements, many do not. This creates an unnecessary problem for applicants. You find a position that matches your experience and capabilities, submit an application, and potentially progress to a telephone or Teams conversation, only to discover that the salary is considerably below your expectations or financial requirements. That means both the applicant and the employer have invested time in a process that could potentially have been avoided. My suggestion is simple: every job advertisement should include a salary or, at the very least, an indicative salary range. A final thought Looking for employment is already a demanding process, particularly when you have been doing so for an extended period. A little more communication, transparency and consideration from employers and recruiters would make LinkedIn a much better platform for everyone involved. These are simply observations from my own experience, shared in the hope that they might make a difference to someone else's job search. Sometimes, improving the experience doesn't require major changes. It simply requires better communication and a little more consideration. #LinkedIn #JobSearch #Recruitment #CareerOpportunities #SalaryTransparency … more

posts.text: If you have employees in California, now is a good time to start reviewing your policies, handbooks, and HR practices. A few changes worth having on your radar: 🔹 Bereavement Leave: Expanded coverage to include designated persons who have a family-like relationship with the employee. 🔹 AI & Workplace Surveillance: New restrictions on using AI to predict or recognize employees' emotional states, collect neural data, and surveillance in workplace bathrooms. 🔹 Employee Protections: Expanded protections involving immigration-related retaliation and clarified definitions of sex discrimination, including pregnancy-related conditions. 🔹 Pay Transparency & Reporting: Updated pay data reporting requirements for larger employers. 🔹 AI & Layoff Notices: Additional disclosure requirements when AI or automation contributes to qualifying mass layoffs or terminations. 🔹 Minimum Wage: California's statewide minimum wage will increase to $17.40/hour, bringing the minimum exempt salary threshold to $72,384 annually. Local minimum wages may be higher. 🔹 Stay-or-Pay Agreements: California's restrictions will apply to agreements entered into on or after January 1, 2027, with expanded exceptions. And that's just the highlight reel! There are also updates affecting privacy regulations, agricultural wages, and San Francisco paid parental leave. 💡 My HR takeaway: Don't wait until January to get ahead of compliance. Review your employee handbook, compensation practices, leave policies, and any technology your organization uses to make employment-related decisions. A compliant workplace isn't just about checking boxes. It's about staying informed, protecting your organization, and making sure employees are treated fairly. HR friends, add this one to your 2027 compliance checklist! 😉 #HumanResources #CaliforniaEmploymentLaw #HRCompliance #PeopleAndCulture #EmploymentLaw #HRLeadership … more

posts.text: In my last article I asked why poverty fell in Timor-Leste and admitted I did not know. A reader pushed me to look at the politics rather than the economics, so I went back through the state budget, a World Bank study I worked on, and my own focus groups. What I found: our domestic revenue covers about one-eighth of what the state spends, and our salary bill alone is now bigger than everything the Petroleum Fund can sustainably provide. The oil was not only paying for development. It was paying for our politics — the settlements, the jobs, the contracts that kept the peace after 2006. Both bills now fall due together. And the generation that will carry them told us last year, in six locations, that they cannot get into the room. In September they stood outside it instead. #TimorLeste #Youth #Governance #PublicFinance #Transparency #Leadership … more

posts.text: Disappointing Recruitment Experience with TCS – A Candidate's Perspective I never expected the recruitment process of an organisation like TCS to be this frustrating and disappointing. My interview process (2 technical and 1 managerial) was completed around 9 September 2026. As of 3 November 2026, nearly 2 months (1 month and 25 days) have passed, and I am still dealing with uncertainty around compensation, work location and the recruitment process. After successfully clearing the technical and managerial rounds, I was informed that I had been selected. I submitted the required documents and patiently followed up for the next steps, expecting the process to move forward professionally. However, the compensation discussions became a series of repeated changes. During the initial discussion, I communicated my expectation of a 62.5% hike over my current CTC. Following negotiations, I agreed to a 56.25% hike. I was subsequently informed that this compensation was being considered, and a salary breakup was even shared. Later, I was told that the proposed compensation was not approved. Despite this, I remained flexible and further revised my expectation to a 37.5% hike to keep the opportunity moving forward. After all these discussions and adjustments, the latest proposal communicated to me represents only a 12.5% hike. The work location added to the uncertainty. Kolkata was initially communicated during the discussion, but later I was told that it was tentative and that another location might be required. What is most frustrating is not just the final offer, but the entire recruitment experience. Candidates invest time in preparing for multiple interview rounds, submit personal documents, attend discussions, make career plans and sometimes put other opportunities on hold based on the information communicated by recruiters. Repeated changes, prolonged delays, lack of timely updates and inconsistent communication make the experience extremely disappointing. I genuinely respected TCS as an organisation and was interested in joining. However, I believe candidates deserve transparency, accountability and clear communication throughout the hiring process. I hope the recruitment leadership takes this feedback seriously and reviews how candidates are being treated during recruitment. Tata Consultancy Services TCS #TCS #CandidateExperience #RecruitmentProcess #HiringExperience #Transparency #Professionalism … more

posts.text: I run reesmarx europe, and for over 30 years we’ve helped US/ Asian and UK/European companies hire across the UK, Europe and Asia. Here are five worth knowing before you make your first hire: Germany: if you need to let someone go, the letter has to be on paper with a handwritten signature. An email or DocuSign won’t count. Germany: a non-compete only holds up if you pay the person at least half their salary for as long as it runs. Netherlands: if an employee is off sick, you could be paying at least 70% of their salary for up to two years. France: contracts and company policies need to be in French. English-only versions can come back to bite you. Across the EU: new pay transparency rules mean salary ranges up front and no asking candidates what they earned before. Each country is bringing this in on its own timetable, so it’s worth checking where you’re hiring. GDPR. Data rules apply to candidate data too, so even CVs held in a US-based applicant tracking system come under them. None of this should put anyone off. UK/Europe are great markets. posts.text: Before you accept an offer, vet the salary. Finding reliable data can be hard. You can find lots of advice on negotiation. But successful negotiations depend on having accurate data. “Should I negotiate?” isn’t the question. You should! You will never have more leverage. And to do that properly, you need facts. (You can get the quick guide I pulled together on finding salary data here: [link hidden] Here are 8 sources of salary data you can check out to make sure you are aiming for the right number. 1.BLS OEWS - [link hidden] This is the best baseline for nearly any role. It’s survey data from employers, with percentiles (10th through 90th) by occupation, metro area, state, and industry. LIMITS: Reports base wages only, job categories are broad, and the data can be 6 to 18 months old. 2. O*Net - [link hidden] Helpful for finding the right job, job outlook, and ranges by location. Better UX than BLS. LIMITS: Its wage figures come from BLS, and several O*NET titles share one BLS number, so it can lack specificity for some jobs. 3. State Pay Transparency Job Postings Many states require job postings to include current market rates in states. Looking at comparable roles in those states can give you a range. LIMITS: Employers may post wide ranges. Not always translatable to other locations. 4. Glassdoor/Indeed You can find info with company-specific numbers LIMITS: Self-reported. Data can be thin for small companies and niche roles. 5. Payscale. com/[link hidden] These sites adjust pay scales by experience, education and skills LIMITS: Modeled estimates that can look more exact than they are. 6. Levels.fyi Info on total compensation at tech and large employers LIMITS: Overstates pay for most other industries. Often includes equity, so the base may be unclear. 7. H1B/DOL Foreign Labor Certification Data Center [link hidden] and [link hidden] Actual base salaries paid by specific employers, required by law for foreign nationals on H1B visas. Prevailing wages are set at four levels, which is a rough proxy for seniority. LIMITS: Only covers sponsored roles. Skews toward big tech and consulting. 8. Professional Associations These groups often report pay in your own field (legal, healthcare, HR, nonprofit and others) LIMITS: Some survey data requires membership or a fee. The best way to approach finding salary data you can rely on is to check several sites so you can feel confident about the range. Most importantly, get the company’s starting number in writing, and be prepared to negotiate for what you deserve! I pulled together these details for you in a simple two-page pdf. posts.text: In France, a job's level is negotiated by the industry. In Romania, each employer decides. EU Pay Transparency in Romania | Directive (EU) 2023/970 asks employers to compare work of equal value on four criteria: skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions. France and Romania start from very different places. FRANCE: THE GRID IS NEGOTIATED → Each industry agreement sets a job classification. In metallurgy, since January 2024, every job is scored on 6 criteria and placed in 1 of 18 classes, each with its own minimum salary. → The Labour Code (art. L2241-15) makes industries review their classifications at least every 5 years and remove criteria that could discriminate between women and men. → Group systems (Hay, Mercer, WTW) sit on top, but each grade must map onto an industry class. ROMANIA: THE GRID IS UP TO YOU → COR gives every job a 6-digit code, mandatory in the contract and in REGES-ONLINE. It names the occupation. It says nothing about level or pay. → Industry agreements are rare, and they set a pay floor, not a grid. Banking: 4,500 lei minimum. Construction: 4,582 lei, plus 3% for skilled work. → So grading lives in each company's own pay system, often a global grade imported from headquarters. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR FRENCH GROUPS IN ROMANIA 1. The French grade has been tested against a negotiated, gender-reviewed grid. The Romanian one usually has not. 2. A COR code is not an equal-value group. Jobs with different codes can be work of equal value. 3. The Directive does not hand you a grid either. Article 4 asks that your own pay structures rest on objective, gender-neutral criteria. The EU toolkit on gender-neutral job evaluation (EIGE and the European Commission) is a free starting point: four factors, three methods by company size. My advice: map your group grades to your Romanian jobs now, and test the criteria before the law makes you. If you work in a French group in Romania: do your grades come from France or were they built locally? #PayTransparency #EqualPay #Romania #HR #LabourLaw #JobEvaluation … more

posts.text: 𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗞𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀: 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗴𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁? 🇭🇰✈️ Over coffee last week with a local Managing Director, he threw a frustrated question my way: "We offer high salaries, low tax rates, and a world-class lifestyle. Why are our international transferees still burning out in year one?" It hit on something I see all the time in international mobility. When bringing top talent to Hong Kong, companies often nail the 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘀-the visas, the housing stipends, the relocation packages. Where things fall apart is in the 𝗺𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼-𝗳𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: ❌ Navigating competitive international school admissions under tight deadlines. ❌ Onboarding a partner or spouse who feels isolated without a career network. ❌ Cultural friction between global leadership styles and local team dynamics. A relocation isn't just a physical move; it's a massive life transition. When an employee spends their first 90 days stressed about family integration or administrative hurdles, they aren't focusing on driving growth for your business. The most successful HK corporates aren't just moving people-they’re building 𝟯𝟲𝟬° 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁-𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗲𝘀 that support the whole family, not just the employee. If you’re hiring or relocating global leadership to HK this year, ask yourself: Are you just paying for the move, or are you setting them up to stay? Let’s chat in the comments 👇 What’s the biggest challenge your organization faces when onboarding international talent in Hong Kong? #GrospironMobilitySolutions #GlobalMobility #HongKongBusiness #HRLeadership #TalentRetention #ExecutiveSearch #FutureOfWork

posts.text: If Harvard can reject brilliant students, why should a business hire someone just for an excellent CV? What exactly qualifies you for a role? Let me share a story. Sometime ago, we shared an opening for a female mathematics tutor. One lady applied, and her application was impressive. Excellent CV. Very good introduction video. Plus certification in teaching mathematical concepts using pictures and visual representations. Now, this caught my attention. At BKB Learning Hub, we work with children who learn differently. So, this lady looked like someone who could add value. We shortlisted her, and I scheduled a call with her. During our discussion, I learned she was already teaching in a physical school. And please, don't get me wrong. There is nothing wrong with teaching in a physical school. In fact, I intend to own one. But I needed to understand her schedule. So I asked about her availability in the evenings. She explained that she already had some tutoring commitments after school. Now, think about this. You finish your regular teaching job around 4 p.m. You take additional lessons between 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. Then you prepare for another class at 9, 10 or even 11 p.m. because you are teaching children in the United States. Depending on your schedule, you could finish teaching at 1a.m or 2 a.m. And then? You still have to wake up around 5:30 or 6 a.m. to prepare for your regular teaching job. Ah! You see, teaching is mental work. It requires concentration, patience, preparation, and keen observation. You are not just opening a textbook and reading to a child. How do you consistently give a child that level of attention when you are already exhausted? Now, you might say, "But Mrs Light, don't you also work at night?" Of course I do! There are nights I finish working at 3 a.m., 4 a.m., sometimes even 6 a.m. On some crazy days, I don't sleep until 8 a.m. But here is the difference. I have the flexibility to sleep during the day. If I finish working at 4 a.m., I can arrange my schedule to get enough rest. Many of our tutors also have that flexibility. They can teach at night and rest during the day. So, after considering her commitments and the demands of the role, I decided, not her. Why? Because I wasn't convinced that she would give our learners the attention they deserve. Then, sometime ago, I came across a write-up asking if a teacher should be rejected because they have a 9 to 5 job. And I thought. Does being qualified automatically mean you are suitable for every opportunity? A good CV or an excellent interview? Because at the end of the day, we are not just hiring someone who knows mathematics. We are hiring someone who will be responsible for a child's learning. Now, over to you. Would you say I was right to turn her down, or should I have given her a chance? I genuinely want to read your comments.

posts.text: November QS Market Predictions | What’s next for the Quantity Surveying market? As we head into November, there are a few trends I expect to see shaping the Quantity Surveying market across Australia. My predictions: 1. Demand for experienced QS professionals will remain competitive. Particularly those who can confidently manage projects from feasibility and cost planning through to final account. 2. Businesses will become more strategic with hiring. Rather than simply increasing headcount, consultancies will be looking for individuals who can add immediate value, strengthen existing teams and support future project pipelines. 3. Salary expectations will continue to be a key conversation. With experienced QS professionals in demand, businesses will need to ensure their remuneration packages reflect the current market. 4. Technical ability won't be enough. Communication, commercial awareness, client management and the ability to build strong relationships will continue to separate good QS professionals from great ones. 5. The lead-up to 2027 will drive hiring conversations. Businesses that start planning their workforce requirements now will be better positioned to secure quality talent ahead of the new year. One thing remains consistent: the best Quantity Surveyors are rarely on the market for long. For consultancies, understanding the market and having the right conversations early will be key to attracting and retaining the right people. What's one trend you're expecting to see in the QS market heading into the new year? #QuantitySurveying #Construction #Recruitment #CostManagement #AustralianConstruction

posts.text: An Employer of Record (EOR) can make a remote architect legally employable. It cannot tell you whether that architect can deliver. posts.text: We're hiring a Senior Workplace Strategy Manager to work with one of our real estate clients in Hong Kong. This is a hands-on role where you will own space supply, capacity and demand across a large building and campus portfolio. You will be the person leadership turns to for clear occupancy plans, smart use of data, and practical advice on how the portfolio should evolve as the business grows. You will develop occupancy plans, coordinate moves at both group and individual level, and work closely with leadership, finance and project teams to keep headcount forecasts aligned with the space strategy. You will also use utilization data to shape better workplace solutions and serve as the client's subject-matter expert on space policies and planning standards. We are looking for someone with a bachelor's degree in real estate, finance, architecture, design or a related field, plus 5 to 7 years of corporate experience. Ideally that experience includes strategic space or occupancy planning. Advanced Excel and AutoCAD skills are essential, and CAFM experience would be a clear advantage. You should also be a strong communicator who is comfortable working with senior stakeholders. This role tends to suit people who have already worked on office portfolio planning, whether that came from a real estate consultancy or from a facilities management or workplace strategy background with solid space-planning exposure. posts.text: I read about a hiring event this week that worked very differently from anything I have seen so far. On Monday, the Philippines' Department of Migrant Workers and the Croatian Employment Service signed recruitment procedures and opened 785 hospitality jobs in Croatia to Filipino workers, for roles like hotel staff, chefs, waiters and housekeeping. Nine Croatian hotel employers came to interview applicants in person, and 943 people were shortlisted. The agreement covers how the recruiting works along with legal and security protections for the workers who go. What I keep thinking about is how much of the work I would have expected an agency to handle, like shortlisting candidates and setting the ground rules, was taken on by two governments here. I am still very new to international recruiting, so I honestly do not know whether this is common or unusual. For those of you who have placed people across borders, does an agreement like this make your job easier because the rules are clear, or does it take away work that used to go to recruiters?

posts.text: Am I about to confuse all of you with my different posts? Maybe? No, I think you're all smarter than that. 😉 Niche-ing, fitting into a box was never really my thing. OK, the umbrella is HOSPITALITY & YACHTING, and underneath that come many things: • Service & Hospitality Coaching • Yacht Crew Training & Education • Communication & Leadership And so on... And collaborating with others in the industry will always be part of what I do. Which brings me to this CV workshop, in collaboration with Yacht Maritime. Lucy spent years working in yachting and now works in recruitment. We got talking, and the topic of how poor so many CVs are here came up. For years, I was also responsible for hiring yacht crew for our fleet, and honestly, some of the CVs were shockingly basic. A Word document or Europass CV might get you by locally, but it doesn't necessarily cut it in the international yachting scene. This isn't a judgement, it's just a reality. Your CV is your first impression. Your passport to the industry. And a lot of people are missing out on opportunities simply because their CV isn't showcasing them properly. The good news? That's an easy fix, WHEN you know how. Continuing to raise the standard in hospitality and yachting is what I am about. And that will come in big and small ways. From conversations and networking, to workshops like this, to my private education and consulting work. So, if you're new to yachting, looking to break into the international market, or an experienced crew member who knows their CV could do with some attention, join us at our workshop in Split. This one will be particularly valuable if you're looking to take that next step in your yachting career. New season. New opportunities. Better CV. DM to learn more.

posts.text: Three months unemployed, and I’m still looking for my next opportunity. These past few months have been a rollercoaster. Interviews come and go. Some go so well that I walk out thinking, “This could be it.” I get invited to the next round, then the next, and I let myself hope. Then the email arrives: “We’ve decided to move forward with other candidates.” Or sometimes: “We’ve decided to pause hiring for this role for now.” I’d be lying if I said it doesn’t sting. Every rejection is a little disappointing, and the bank account is bleeding a little more each month. But I’ve learned that every one of them tells a story too. It’s rarely about ability. More often it’s about fit, timing, or what a company needs at that moment. Sometimes the role itself changes before anyone is hired. Each interview has sharpened how I tell my story, and each “no” has pointed me closer to the right “yes”. So I’m not giving up. I’ll keep applying, keep learning, and keep showing up. I’m looking for Office Manager or Admin & Operation Specialists roles in Singapore, where my 20+ years across office management, HR, finance and vendor management can make a real difference. If you know of an opening, or can introduce me to someone hiring, I’d be grateful. A referral, a bit of advice or a quick chat would mean a lot. And to everyone who is job hunting too, I see you. posts.text: “We can discuss the work arrangement at the interview.” That sentence can leave an important part of your hiring brief unresolved. For Singapore employers, workspace planning affects more than office capacity. It shapes who considers the role, what recruiters screen for and whether the eventual offer matches the candidate’s expectations. Before sourcing begins, clarify three things. Where will the work happen? Specify the actual work location, expected office attendance and any travel between sites. If hybrid work is available, explain the arrangement and any conditions. “Flexible” should mean something both sides can understand. What does the role need? A client-facing employee, an operations coordinator and a specialist doing focused work may need different setups. Define the requirements around customer access, collaboration, equipment and privacy. Connect attendance expectations to the work involved. Does the setup support your hiring plan? Separate the vacancy you need to fill now from future headcount plans. Confirm who the new hire reports to, where onboarding happens and whether the workspace and equipment will be ready for the intended start date. Then carry those decisions through the recruitment process: CLARIFY Put the location, work arrangement, role outcomes and reporting line into one agreed brief. SHORTLIST Assess candidates against the actual requirements, including whether the working arrangement suits them. DECIDE Keep interviewers aligned, respond promptly and make sure the offer reflects what was discussed. For example, if a role requires daily attendance at an Ubi office and regular client visits, explain both upfront. Candidates can then assess the opportunity with a clearer understanding of the job. If the arrangement is still being decided, say so clearly. Hyer Talents supports Singapore employers with structured hiring briefs, relevant shortlists and responsive interview coordination. A clearer brief gives everyone a better basis for the next decision. Hiring in Singapore? #hiring Senior Audit Associate

Apply here: https://lnkd.in/gTqCiQiC

Job Description If youre going to leave a firm youre perfectly happy at, the next one needs to give you a few good reasons.  This one does.  Theyre an Indianapolis-based CPA firm of around 40 people, currently growing and moving into a bigger space. Theyve had opportunities to grow much faster through mergers, but that isnt really what they want.  Theyd rather keep the feel of a smaller firm and grow by hiring good people.  And right now, they particularly need experienced people in the middle of the team.  As an Audit Senior, youd work across a varied client base including construction, manufacturing, nonprofit, and public sector organizations. Youll be involved across engagements, working directly with clients and taking on more responsibility as you progress.  Its a good place for someone who wants to keep learning without feeling like theyre one of 100 Seniors all waiting for the same promotion.  They do want people in the office and on site for certain engagements, particularly because they put a lot of emphasis on training. But theyre sensible about what flexibility actually means.  Busy season is around 55 hours, and Saturdays can be worked from home. Outside of busy season, youre generally back to a normal 40-hour week.  If youve got children, a doctors appointment or just something you need to sort during the day, theyll work around it. Nobody needs to make their dentist appointment sound like a national emergency.  There are some good practical benefits too.  They cover 90% of your parking costs, theres a workout facility in the building and food available in the canteen. Theyve also introduced a 30 minute mental health break during the working day.  One of the more unusual benefits is what happens when you work additional hours.  Once you go beyond their annual hours threshold, extra hours can start converting into additional vacation time. Around 200 hours above that threshold works out at roughly another week of PTO.  Theyre looking for someone with solid public accounting audit experience whos ready to step into a Senior level role. You dont need to have your CPA already, although itll become important if you want to progress into management later on.  You might be quite comfortable where you are.  But if you could move somewhere that stays relatively small, gives you room to progress, and makes busy season a little easier to live with, it might be worth seeing what else is out there.  If youre just browsing the job boards and you havent dusted off your resume yet, thats not a problem. If youve read this advert and youre unsure whether to apply because you dont have every bit of experience listed, Id still encourage you to apply. They will be responsible for researching and developing CLPHA’s positions on a range of policies including public housing, Housing Choice Vouchers, preservation and redevelopment, and economic mobility.

“We are thrilled to welcome Isaac, Lesley, and Chandler to the CLPHA team,” said La Shelle Dozier, CEO of CLPHA. “They each bring deep expertise to their positions. Their energy and enthusiasm for advancing CLPHA’s mission to serve our PHA members and their residents will be a tremendous asset as we navigate the challenges facing public and affordable housing. Please join me in welcoming them to the team.”

Isaac Dozier comes to Housing Is from the U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development (HUD), where he led more than $100 million in public-private partnership initiatives connecting public housing authorities, developers, and community organizations to HUD’s redevelopment priorities as the Senior Project Manager, Neighborhood and Community Investment for the Jobs Plus Program. Before HUD, Isaac was the Director of Community Development for the Housing Authority of the City of Fort Myers, Florida, Regional Vice President of Urban Strategies, Inc., and Director of Client Services for the Housing Authority of New Orleans. Isaac also previously served in the U.S. Army and holds an MBA from American Inter-Continental University and a BA from the University of Texas at El Paso.

Lesley Freiman is a policy and strategy leader with more 15 years of experience advancing housing stability, economic mobility, community health and family well-being through cross-sector partnerships, implementation support, organizational learning, and capacity building. Prior to joining CLPHA, Lesley was an associate at Abt Global, where she directed research, evaluation, and technical assistance initiatives for federal and nonprofit clients. Lesley holds a Master of Public Policy from the University of Michigan's Ford School and a bachelor's degree from Brown University.

Chandler Ian Wilkins, PhD, is a housing policy researcher with experience studying the intersection of federal housing policy, disaster recovery, and community resilience. He previously served as a research associate at the Urban Institute, where he led and contributed to federally and philanthropically funded research on housing resilience, disaster preparedness, flood mitigation in subsidized housing, and equitable community resilience planning. Chandler holds a PhD in Urban and Regional Science and a Master of Urban Planning from Texas A&M University, as well as a Bachelor of Science in Community and Regional Planning from Iowa State University.

posts.text:
A seasonal hire's first Black Friday shift often decides whether they come back for a second one.

Picture it: 10 a.m., the queue is already at the door, and an associate who joined three days ago gets a radio and one instruction: "Just help where it's busy."

By noon they're lost. By closing time, they've decided retail isn't for them.

Now picture the same person getting 15 minutes before opening:
→ One zone that's theirs for the day
→ One buddy they can call on the radio
→ One clear answer to "What do I do if I don't know?"

Same store. Same crowd. A very different shift.

This year it matters even more. Challenger, Gray & Christmas expects U.S. seasonal retail hiring to fall again, to about 450,000 jobs, as retailers lean more on their existing teams (via Retail Dive). Fewer new hires means each one counts more.

The cheapest retention tool in retail is a good first shift.

What's the one thing you make sure every new hire knows before their first peak day? 👇

posts.text:
Retail Christmas hiring is quieter this year. You can see it in the numbers.

KPMG and the REC found retail had the steepest drop in demand for permanent staff of any sector in October. John Lewis is taking on 10,400 seasonal staff, down from 13,700 last year. BRC has retail sales up 1.5% in October, with non-food flat while people wait for Black Friday.

Then there's the longer view. LinkedIn data shared at Hire Connect puts UK retail hiring 24% below pre-pandemic levels, and the National Living Wage goes up to £13.21 next April. I don't blame any retailer for thinking twice about every role.

My worry is what that caution does to the hires that do go ahead. Once a head office team has been trimmed back, a good buyer or area manager carries a lot more weight. Get it wrong and you feel it for a long time.

That's where we try to earn our keep at Tandem. We'd rather send two people we've properly checked than ten CVs, and we stay in touch once they've started.

If you're in retail, are you holding back for 2027 or trying to get ahead of everyone else?

posts.text:
Beyond Filling Seats: The Real Mass Recruitment Challenge in Thailand’s F&B Retail 

In Thailand’s hyper-competitive F&B retail space, store expansion is fast, margins are tight, and customer expectations are unforgiving. Scaling a frontline workforce at the speed of business, without sacrificing service quality, requires more than a traditional volume-hiring approach.

Here is what is actually happening on the ground right now, and how our people strategy needs to pivot:

1. Speed Wins the Talent War
Frontline candidates have endless options, from gig economy platforms to rival chains opening right next door. A 3-day gap between an interview and an offer is all it takes to lose great talent.
• The Shift: Moving toward same-day hiring, mobile-first applications (via LINE), and frictionless onboarding.

2. Early Turnover is a Store P&L Issue
Losing a seasoned crew member isn't just an HR metric. It directly impacts peak-hour speed, product consistency, and regular customer retention. Meanwhile, Store Managers get trapped in a cycle of constant firefighting and retraining.
• The Shift: Recruitment doesn't end at contract signing. Partnering closely with Area Managers to fix the first 30 days through structured buddy systems and realistic job previews is where the real ROI lies.

3. Competing Beyond Hourly Rates
Offering a slightly higher base wage is easily copied by competitors. Today’s frontline workforce stays for flexibility, visible micro-career paths (e.g., Crew to Shift Supervisor in 6 months), and supportive leadership.
• The Shift: Equipping Store Managers to be coaches, not just shift schedulers. People join for the pay, but they stay for their Store Manager.

Mass recruitment in F&B isn't about lowering the bar to fill rosters. It is about re-engineering how we attract, onboard, and retain talent at scale.

posts.text:
‘Unwanted staff’….Has Inside Retail Australia become The Sun UK?!
 
  
Clickbait at the cost of other people’s wellbeing is a low blow. 
  
Here’s the stats to save the click:
  
50% of DJ’s stores are closing, 1,689 roles being made redundant, only 170 staff being offered other roles. 1,519 staff members ‘unwanted’. 
  
People have lost their roles because of poor decisions on store locations not attracting the right customer, not because of the customer facing team on the floor.  

David Jones has high standards of hiring. For everyone effected by this, I’m sorry. There’s panic, shock and sadness to process, but there are plenty of retailers out there who would LOVE to bring your knowledge of high end, luxury product and service into their brand. 
   
Get your CV ready showing your achievements (KPIs), get onto Seek and get onto Linkedin. 
  
Your next role might not be your ‘dream job’ but it’s an opportunity to try something new.

posts.text:
WE ARE NOT THE SAME. 📢

Companies REALLY need to stop 🛑 hiring for DTC AND Amazon as though they’re the same job.

Yes, they’re both ecommerce and involve selling products online, but the platforms, operational requirements, knowledge base, and strategic priorities are VERY different ⚠️

DTC requires expertise in website management, customer acquisition, conversion optimization, retention, email marketing, and the overall customer experience.

Amazon requires expertise in marketplace operations, catalog architecture, inventory management, platform compliance, advertising, profitability, and navigating a system where Amazon controls the rules.

These are two completely different environments that should complement each other, not be run the same way.

Yet I constantly see job descriptions expecting ONE person to be an expert in both, usually with a salary that barely covers the expertise required for one 🤡.

Don’t get me wrong, a senior ecommerce leader can absolutely oversee both channels, but overseeing and personally executing are VERY different responsibilities.

If you want someone who can personally execute both at an expert level, understand how rare that combination is… start hiring one for each instead. 🦄

IS YOUR CV ACTUALLY READY FOR TODAY'S RECRUITMENT PROCESS?

Having professional experience and skills is important. But how effectively does your CV communicate them?

Let's look at two different CV approaches.

01. NON-ATS-FRIENDLY CV
A CV with poor formatting, inconsistent structure, unclear sections or inappropriate layouts may create difficulties for recruiters and Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS).

02. ATS-FRIENDLY CV
A professionally structured CV focuses on:
Clean and consistent formatting.
Relevant industry-specific keywords.
Clearly organised work experience.
Proper presentation of skills and qualifications.
Readability and ATS-conscious structure.

BUT THERE IS MORE THAN JUST ONE CV FORMAT!

I have explored and developed 15+ different ATS-friendly CV layout and structure ideas, drawing inspiration from CV approaches used by professionals across the Logistics and Supply Chain industry.

Different job roles require different ways of presenting professional experience. A Warehouse Executive's CV, a Transportation Coordinator's CV and a Supply Chain Executive's CV should not necessarily follow identical content structures.

Senior Logistics Manager Interview Preparation Questions

Target Countries: USA | UK | Canada | UAE | Australia | India

Experience Level: 10+ Years of Experience

1 How do you develop and implement a comprehensive logistics strategy that aligns with overall business objectives while optimizing transportation, warehousing, and distribution costs?

2. How do you manage end-to-end supply chain logistics operations, ensuring timely deliveries, inventory accuracy, and operational efficiency across multiple locations?

3. What KPIs do you use to measure logistics performance, and how do you improve metrics such as OTIF, order cycle time, freight cost per unit, and delivery accuracy?

4. Describe how you negotiate and manage strategic relationships with third-party logistics (3PL) providers, freight forwarders, and transportation partners to achieve cost efficiency and service excellence.

5. How do you handle major supply chain disruptions, transportation delays, port congestion, or unexpected capacity constraints while minimizing business impact?

6 What strategies have you implemented to reduce logistics and transportation costs without compromising customer satisfaction or delivery performance?

7How do you leverage ERP systems, Warehouse Management Systems (WMS), Transportation Management Systems (TMS), and data analytics to improve logistics visibility and decision-making?

8. How do you ensure compliance with international trade regulations, customs procedures, import/export documentation, and cross-border transportation requirements?

9. Describe a situation where you led a major logistics transformation or process improvement initiative. What challenges did you face, and what measurable results did you achieve?

10 As a Senior Logistics Manager, how do you lead large, cross-functional teams, manage departmental budgets, develop talent, and align logistics operations with long-term organizational growth?

This time of year, you see a lot of supply chain & logistics salary data published. 

This is especially worth noting since salary bands have been trending up. 

I see this when talking to candidates, but also when talking to supply chain hiring authorities.  

Recently, a VP of Supply Chain told me about a demand planning leader role they needed to backfill.  

They haven’t had to hire a demand planner in 5 years, and they were surprised by how much market salaries have risen during this time.  

I had a conversation with a Chief Procurement Officer who was close to making an offer for a Strategic Sourcing Manager role.  

It turns out they significantly underestimated the salary the candidate was seeking, and thus needed to get approval to increase the budget for this role.  
The moral of the story is that supply chain workers are expected to do more for their organization.  

This means overseeing larger budgets, tracking more performance measures, and managing more cross-functional initiatives.  

Fortunately, most companies know they need to pay a premium to not only recruit top talent, but also keep top talent in their seats.

posts.text:
We changed the title from Commodity Manager to Strategic Sourcing Manager, and this is why titles are the trickiest part of supply chain hiring.

They couldn't find the right person for this role for about a year.

When they came to us, we learned they needed someone with management experience to lead their buying team.

Two of their buyers had recently retired, and their commodity manager was close to retiring.

We changed the title because:

1. Commodity Manager sounds like a solo role: one person who owns a category. So it attracted candidates without management experience.

2. Strategic Sourcing Manager tells candidates the job includes managing buyers and broader sourcing.

This is one of the reasons companies can't fill a role.

The titles they're using are attracting the wrong profiles.

If you're not sure which title to use:

1. Get clear on what the person will own day to day.

2. If they'll manage people, make sure the title says so.

3. Check that the job description matches the real level of responsibility.

posts.text:
It would surprise most people how few domestic suppliers large U.S. companies actually use nowadays.

Even for products assembled here, the raw materials and components often come from Brazil, Thailand, Vietnam, or somewhere else entirely. After adding freight and transportation costs, the quality and the price still come out ahead. The old picture of a procurement team calling a raw material supplier down the road doesn’t match how the job works anymore.

That’s a big part of why supply chain talent is so hard to find. The leaders companies need have to understand sourcing across countries, regulations, and freight lanes and they have to do it while tariffs and geopolitical events are ever changing.

When we screen for these roles, one of the first things we want to know is where a candidate has actually sourced from and how they reacted to a change in supply, new tariffs and new geopolitical events.

Supply Chain and Procurement professionals have to be agile, quick on their feet, fortune tellers, and creative solvers. Those are the candidates companies pay us to find!

I knew nothing about working in supply chain when I walked into my interviews.
What I did have was audacity, and a very real need for a new iPhone.
I was young, I was just out of college, and I needed a job. So I applied everywhere and went to random interviews, fully convinced it would all work out somehow.
Two companies said no.
One said yes.
And it was the one that matched my audacity.
Today I’m a supply chain analyst, and I’ve learned a lot since then. But here’s what I took from it:

→ You don’t need to know everything to start. You need to be willing to learn fast.
→ Rejections are redirections.
→ Confidence gets you in the room. Curiosity keeps you there.

And yes, I did get the iPhone.

What you’ll do Supply chain planning 

Execute the plant-level supply chain strategy to ensure continuous material availability for production. 

Participate in monthly and weekly S&OP/IBP cycles, aligning production, inventory and logistics with business demand. 

Warehousing & logistics 

Manage RM, PM and FG warehousing for optimal space utilisation and full statutory, safety and quality compliance. 

Drive efficiency in inbound and outbound logistics and maintain service-level adherence. 

Manage internal and external logistics partners for timely, cost-effective material movement. 

Vendor & procurement 

Manage procurement of direct and indirect materials in partnership with central procurement. 

Ensure timely renewal of AMC/CAMC, plant service contracts (canteen, security, employee transport), and logistics and warehousing agreements. 

Build strong relationships with local suppliers, transporters and contractors, and improve their performance through KPls and scorecards. 

Inventory 

Maintain inventory norms of 4 weeks for RM and 3 weeks for PM. 

Reduce slow-moving and obsolete inventory by 20%, and manage scrap and redundant stock disposal per policy. 

Conduct periodic inventory audits for accuracy and compliance. 

Budget & cost 

Build the annual supply chain budget across procurement, logistics and warehousing, and ensure adherence across warehousing, freight, COGS, co-packing and related cost heads. 

Lead continuous improvement projects delivering ~2% budgeted savings without compromising service or compliance. 

Compliance & safety 

Ensure 100% adherence to statutory requirements, company SOPs, audit standards and EHS frameworks, including Gemba and safety schedules. 

Maintain accurate records of material movement, vendor contracts and purchases.

MBA in Supply Chain Management / Operations

posts.text:
WHAT CEOs SHOULD KNOW BEFORE HIRING A SUPPLY CHAIN DIRECTOR

The wrong supply chain decision can affect far more than delivery. So why do companies still evaluate supply chain leaders primarily on cost and efficiency?

A candidate promises lower inventory, faster delivery, and better supplier pricing. Impressive. But is that enough to lead your supply chain?

Not necessarily.

Today's Supply Chain Director influences working capital, customer experience, operational resilience, and business growth.

A lower purchasing price may increase supply risk. Leaner inventory may improve cash flow but reduce service reliability. Automation may increase productivity without delivering sufficient return on investment.

For CEOs, the hiring decision should go beyond technical expertise.

Look for leaders who can balance cost, risk, service, and growth; collaborate with finance and operations; build supplier resilience; and use data and AI responsibly.

Just as importantly, assess their ability to make decisions under uncertainty—not merely manage established processes.

At ESS Executive, we believe senior hiring should begin with the business outcomes a leader must deliver.

The strongest Supply Chain Director is not simply the person who reduces costs. It is the leader who understands the consequences of every major supply chain decision.

PAMT’s rate per mile was up 11% from the previous quarter. Good news for the freight market, right? 📈

But management also pointed to higher costs for recruiting and retaining qualified drivers, along with fuel costs and lower equipment-sale gains, as pressures offsetting those pricing improvements.

It’s a good reminder that better freight rates don’t magically make qualified drivers easier to find or keep.

A cheap application is great. But how many of those applicants are qualified? How many make it through orientation? And how many are still driving for you 30, 60 or 90 days later?

The cheapest application isn’t always the cheapest hire. And the cheapest hire isn’t always the driver who stays.

Let’s look beyond the application and focus on where our recruiting dollars are actually producing results.

When you sit down to interview an executive overseeing driver recruitment for the Department of Defense’s largest private hauler of hazardous freight, you expect polished corporate talking points. Instead, my 40-minute conversation with Michael Fisk was candid, unfiltered, and compelling.
  
I connected with the Roadmaster Group’s vice president to discuss the tightening market for qualified hazmat and tanker drivers. While the story dives into how federal enforcement and strict safety standards have shrunk the active talent pool to fewer than 10,000 “unicorn” drivers, what really stood out during the interview was Fisk’s no-nonsense pragmatism.
  
He admits that sizing up the driver market is “more an art than a science”—even when you’re spending $1 million a year on recruiting ads to track down qualified talent. Because turnkey liquid haulers are so scarce, Roadmaster recruits on “character and work ethic” first, converting ambitious flatbed drivers and putting them through an intense, two-week orientation in the Arizona heat. (He even invited me out to Glendale to test my mettle in the group’s heavy-duty rubber PPE suits—which sounded a bit too much like Marine boot camp to me.)
  
From hauling military munitions and microchip hazwaste to supporting major environmental cleanups, Fisk’s perspective on why safety can never take a back seat to cheap freight is a must-read.
  
The link to the full story is in the comments. 👇

THE RIGHT TRANSPORTATION COMPLIANCE LEADER CAN SAVE A FORTUNE 500 COMPANY MILLIONS.

Your transportation compliance department isn’t overhead. The right leader can make it one of your company’s most valuable financial safeguards.

From challenging inaccurate FMCSA violations through DataQs to improving CSA performance, reducing insurance exposure, and protecting operating authority, the right individual can potentially safeguard hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue and financial exposure across a major transportation enterprise.

Yet companies continue making one critical mistake: Hiring a résumé instead of hiring proven leadership.

A retired State Trooper or Police Officer, impressive titles, but a wall full of certifications doesn’t automatically translate into effective corporate transportation leadership. Enforcement experience has value, but enforcing regulations and managing a complex nationwide transportation operation are two very different disciplines.

Don’t confuse an impressive career history with the hunger, fire in the belly, commitment, and ability to deliver results. 

Hire someone who has spent years in the trenches. Someone with technical expertise, business instincts, strong industry relationships, people skills, and the fire in their belly to transform an organization’s compliance culture.

And understand something else:

This individual may not be the most popular person in your organization. Nor should you expect them to be.

They’re not there to win a popularity contest, make friends, or tell executives what they want to hear. They’re there to identify risks, challenge complacency, confront uncomfortable truths, and protect the company.

Often highly analytical, extraordinarily detail-oriented, independent, and somewhat reserved, these professionals frequently do their best work away from the spotlight.

They don’t require constant supervision or recognition. They thrive on autonomy, accountability, and measurable results. Some voluntarily work unconventional hours, occasionally putting in 12- to 16-hour days—not because someone demands it, but because they’re deeply invested in their work and driven to deliver results.

Their personality may not command the boardroom, but their results should command its attention.

While others focus on quarterly earnings and operational growth, this individual is often working behind the scenes, protecting the company’s drivers, operating authority, financial stability, and reputation from costly federal, state, and local enforcement actions.

They need to be the person who knows the regulations, understands the operation, earns professional respect, builds a strong culture, and produces undeniable results.

Stop hiring résumés. Start hiring passion, integrity, experience, independence, and proven performance.

Because the right hire can transform an entire transportation organization.
The wrong hire can jeopardize everything you’ve built.

Keeping Trucks Moving Starts Long Before the Driver Turns the Key
Every successful delivery starts with a plan.
The right truck. The right route. The right schedule. And most importantly, the right driver.
For Fleet Managers and Transportation Directors, keeping everything moving isn't always easy.
You're balancing delivery schedules, customer expectations, operating costs, and driver availability. And when something unexpected happens, your entire day can change.
When One Driver Calls Out, Everyone Feels It
Your trucks are loaded, routes are planned, and deliveries are scheduled.
Then a driver calls out.
Now you're rearranging routes, asking other drivers to work overtime, and trying to avoid delivery delays.
Sound familiar?
Driver shortages happen. But having a plan in place can make all the difference.
Planning Ahead Keeps Your Business Moving
Having the right drivers available is just as important as having the right equipment.
Here are three things every transportation leader should consider:
1. Do you have a backup plan?
Vacations, call-outs, and turnover happen. Having access to qualified drivers when needed can help prevent disruptions.
2. Are you relying too much on overtime?
Too much overtime can increase costs, create driver fatigue, and lead to turnover.
3. Can your driver workforce keep up with growth?
New customers and more deliveries are great opportunities, but only if you have enough drivers to support them.
It's About More Than Filling an Empty Seat
At ProDrivers, we understand that finding drivers is only part of the challenge.
What matters most is keeping trucks moving, deliveries on schedule, drivers safe, and customers satisfied.
The goal isn't just to fill an open position. It's to prevent that vacancy from disrupting your business.
I'd Love to Hear From You
Fleet Managers and Transportation Leaders: What's your biggest challenge when it comes to maintaining reliable driver coverage?
Is it unexpected call-outs, turnover, finding qualified drivers, or something else?
I'd welcome your thoughts and experiences. ProDrivers

𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆.

Finding lease-on owner-operators isn’t easy right now.

But needing another truck doesn’t mean every truck is the 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 truck.
We learned that lesson the expensive way.

In the past, we occasionally looked past obvious red flags because we needed capacity. We told ourselves we were giving someone an opportunity.

Then the questions started:

“Can I get an advance?”

“Can the company pay for my truck repair?”

“Can I put tires, equipment or supplies on your account?”

Those questions may not bother everyone.

They bother us.

Not because we’re unwilling to help people, but because experience has taught us where that road can lead.

We’ve ignored the warning signs before.

𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝘂𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀.

So today, we politely end those conversations and move on.

Yes, that means we probably pass on people who might have worked out.

That’s a risk we’re willing to take.

Because one bad lease-on decision can create far more problems than one empty spot on the board.

These days, we hire almost exclusively through referrals.

We’d rather have fewer trucks operated by the right people than more trucks operated by people we knew, deep down, we shouldn’t have brought on board in the first place.

𝗔𝗻 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘆 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

We’ll take the capacity problem.

A job interview, medical appointment, meeting with a parole officer, or visit to a community resource may seem straightforward—until the bus route doesn't reach the destination, the fare is unaffordable, or a promised ride falls through.

Practical planning matters. Mapping the route ahead of time, checking schedules, and allowing extra travel time can help.

But individuals shouldn't have to solve every transportation barrier alone.

Community partners can make a difference by listening, understanding the specific challenge, and helping identify realistic transportation options.

At The Rock Found, we believe successful reentry requires dignity, practical problem-solving, and meaningful community connections.

Real Challenges. Real Solutions. Brighter Futures.

posts.text: 1,000 people 💜 That’s how many clients Aunty Jane has cared for in just over 12 months. I’ve been quiet on here for a long time. posts.text: Over the past few years, I’ve worked with many SMEs across Hong Kong and the APAC region to help them implement AI in practical, real-world ways. Recently, I’ve been hearing the same concern from many business owners: “It’s not that we don’t have enquiries — we just can’t keep up.” Missed calls, slow WhatsApp replies, no-shows after bookings — in the end, it’s often not a demand problem, but a frontline communication capacity problem. In the past few months, I’ve helped several service-based businesses (across education, professional services, medical aesthetics, and local services) redesign their frontline sales and enquiry workflows. Not with flashy AI features, but with a very practical principle: hand repetitive, time-sensitive, accuracy-critical tasks over to systems. One common shift I’ve seen is moving from “hiring people to answer calls and messages” to a 24/7 AI-powered sales assistant handling first-touch interactions. The results these companies have seen are quite consistent: Faster responses and significantly fewer missed enquiries Higher booking completion rates and fewer no-shows Sales teams spending less time chasing leads and more time closing Headcount costs no longer increasing linearly with enquiry volume One client put it well: “It’s not that AI replaced someone — it’s that one person no longer has to do the work of three.” From my perspective, the real value of AI isn’t about how “smart” it looks. It’s about protecting opportunities that already exist but are being lost due to capacity constraints. This is especially relevant for Hong Kong SMEs. If every additional enquiry requires additional manpower, scaling becomes extremely difficult. That’s why systemising, standardising, and running frontline communication 24/7 is often the first and most worthwhile step. Seeing these results repeatedly has reinforced one belief for me: AI doesn’t need to be loud or impressive — it needs to be practical, grounded, and directly tied to business outcomes. If you’re facing similar challenges, or simply want to exchange notes on how SMEs are actually using AI on the ground, I’m always open to a conversation.

posts.text: R10,000 CHANGED AN ENTIRE INDUSTRY. In 1978, Ivan and Lynette Saltzman borrowed R10,000 from Ivan’s mother, Mary, to buy a neglected 75 m² pharmacy in Mondeor, Johannesburg. Ivan had worked there as a locum and knew what he would change. People warned him against buying it. The seller reportedly left their cheque uncashed for almost a year. Within six months, turnover had doubled. Both were pharmacists, but they thought like retailers. Ivan grew up helping in his mother’s shop. They drove to wholesalers for glassware, gifts and everyday essentials. When earrings arrived, customers queued. Ivan sent staff into Pick n Pay to check prices. Other chemists expected their mini-supermarket approach to fail. Instead, the little pharmacy doubled in size. In the early 1980s, they put everything into a second store at Randridge Mall. High rentals had frightened off other retailers. With a young family, it was a huge gamble. Lynette called it their hardest decision; Ivan described those early bets as double or quits. It worked. By their fifth pharmacy, their mothers were telling them to stop. They kept going, sourcing products in Hong Kong and China to keep prices competitive. For years Ivan carried his paperwork between stores in a shopping basket. He even recalled stopping to inspect another pharmacy while driving Lynette to hospital to give birth. Business filled family dinners too, a sacrifice he later acknowledged. Lynette ran the Fourways store, which she recalled turning over R2 million a month, and helped build beauty into a major category. Eventually Ivan couldn’t oversee every store. Selected pharmacists became part-owners, with stakes funded from future profits. They were creating entrepreneurs, not just hiring managers. In 2016, Dis-Chem listed on the JSE at a valuation of roughly R16 billion. It aimed to double its store footprint within five to eight years. By February 2026, the group had 316 pharmacies and 42 baby stores, generating R42.8 billion in annual revenue. Just 38% of retail revenue came from dispensary products. Behind the stores stood a national distribution operation supplying 280 Local Choice pharmacies and 1,325 independent pharmacy customers. The business that challenged traditional chemists had become a supplier to them. But perhaps the greatest test came when it was time to hand over leadership. Rui Morais became CEO in 2023. Ivan and their son Saul left the board in July 2026, completing a planned transition towards professional management. Lynette had already stepped down as an executive director in 2022, while continuing her work in beauty. After 48 years, the business they built no longer depended on its founders to lead it.

posts.text: I went to Masters' Union for an MBA in HR. I landed with a mental health startup instead. 🌙 Not because anyone told me to. Because the education did something unexpected: it made me see gaps. I learned to listen. I learned to see systems. I learned what doesn’t work. I started learning different perspectives: A founder: “I can’t tell anyone I’m burned out.” A CEO: “Therapy costs ₹5,000. My team earns ₹30,000.” A CTO: “My engineers are leaving. I don’t know why.” A CHRO: “Our wellness program isn’t working.” They all said: “There has to be something between suffering alone and paying ₹5,000 for therapy.” There wasn’t. So I built it. 💪 What I Built 🤖 An AI that listens at 2 AM. Not a therapist. Not another meditation app. Not something that says “stay positive.” Here’s what happens: ✅ Open it. No email. No phone. Just you and an AI that reads your mood in every single message. ✅ It reflects back what you said. Specific. Not “that sounds hard.” ✅ Need advice? 2–3 options. Need to vent? It lets you. Need to spiral? It goes there. ✅ Danger? Real helpline numbers (Tele-MANAS 14416, 1-[电话已隐去], 112). You decide. No escalation. ✅ Everything is encrypted. You can delete it all. One tap. ✅ It’s honest: “Hi, I’m an AI. Not a therapist. Not a person.” Launches in 3 days. India-only. Soft launch. 🚀 To every Masters’ Union student reading this: You’re learning to see what others miss. Don’t ignore it. Build something about it. Why This Matters 📊 The gap is brutal: 92% of India has zero mental health access. Therapy: ₹2,000–₹5,000/session. (5–15% of monthly income.) 2 psychiatrists per 100,000 people. 45% of CTOs are burned out. Half will quit without notice. 70% of CHROs say wellness is priority. 40% have zero plan. Peak anxiety: 11 PM – 4 AM. (When therapists sleep.) The solution? Something actually there at 2 AM. Try this next week. Use it. Break it. Tell me if it works. Share it with your team. They need this more than a standing desk. The Real Ask 🤝 Option 1: Reply. Tell me your 2 AM story. Option 2: DM. Get early access. Option 3: Share. Tag someone who needs this. Option 4: CHRO? Let’s talk retention. Option 5: Educator? This is what your students can do. Big thanks to our AI in Business class for teaching me to actually see the gaps.
