posts.text: 'Company for sale: the new 'loneliness industry' in China No country is aging as fast as China: by 2035, there will be more than 400 million people over 65, which is 100 million more than today. Traditionally, it is the duty of adult children to take care of mother and father in their old age. But that system is starting to falter, as more and more Chinese move to the city while their parents stay behind in the countryside. But China is tackling this loneliness epidemic in a creative way. By 'renting' children, for example. Veerle De Vos, journalist at VRT NWS. She specializes in Asia, the United Kingdom and Ireland. AI summary: China is ageing at an unprecedented pace. By 2035, the country is expected to have more than 400 million people aged 65 and over, around 100 million more than today. The traditional Chinese value of filial piety ("xiao"), which emphasises respect and care for one's parents, is under strain. Many younger Chinese move to cities for work, leaving ageing parents behind in rural areas and often seeing them only once a year. Nursing homes remain socially sensitive and are often viewed negatively. China follows a 90-7-3 care model: 90% of older people are cared for at home. 7% receive community-based support. Only 3% live in residential care facilities. As a result, a new "loneliness industry" has emerged. Companies offer services such as "shared children", where paid companions visit elderly people, help with errands, perform small tasks, and provide company. This reflects a broader trend of hiring social and family substitutes. In China, people can also hire fake fiancés, companions, or even stand-in family members for social and family obligations. The commercialisation of family relationships is controversial. An app that offered paid substitutes to visit parents during the Chinese New Year holiday received heavy criticism and quickly withdrew the service. Legal disputes have arisen when elderly people choose to leave part of their inheritance to paid caregivers or "shared children" who provided genuine support and companionship. Technology is increasingly used to bridge the gap between generations. Mobile apps allow adult children to monitor their parents' wellbeing and health remotely. China is also investing heavily in care robots and companion robots capable of conversation, games, reminiscence activities, and some caregiving functions. Researchers believe more advanced versions could be widely deployed around 2030. The article ultimately raises a broader social question: despite China's remarkable economic growth and rising prosperity, why has the country also become increasingly lonely and socially disconnected? Key takeaway: China is responding to rapid ageing, family separation, and loneliness through a combination of commercial companionship services, digital monitoring, and robotics. However, these solutions also challenge traditional ideas about family, care, and human connection.'

posts.text: Most patients never think about who answers when they call their doctor's office. Practice managers think about it all the time. At Call Center Options, our medical receptionists and prior-authorization specialists work full time on a single practice. They learn that practice's EHR, its scheduling rules, its providers' preferences and the insurance plans its patients use, and they follow the notes and instructions the practice keeps in its own system. When something needs a clinician, it goes to the practice's staff the way the practice wants it to. Our team works from our office in Pristina, Kosovo, on virtual desktops hosted in the United States. Patient records stay on U.S. servers and are never stored on computers overseas. Before an agent ever takes a call, they're trained on the practice's systems and procedures. We think that's what lets a small practice offer patients a well-run front desk without hiring and training another local employee every time someone leaves. If your front desk is stretched, I'm happy to compare notes: [link hidden] #MedicalPractice #HealthcareAdministration #PatientExperience #PracticeManagement

posts.text: International recruitment in 2016 vs 2026. Quite a lot’s changed in 10 years! I’ve spent over 17 years helping recruiters move overseas. In 2016, if you’d billed well, worked for a couple of good agencies and were up for packing your bags, you had options. You still do. Where those options are might surprise you. Middle East 🇦🇪 Dubai Fancy Dubai but love the desk you’ve built? Bring it with you. We’re seeing Dubai agencies hire recruiters to run UK, European and US desks from here. If you recruit tech contractors in Benelux or Switzerland, Dubai agencies want that experience. Fancy a new market too? You could use it to build a Gulf contract desk. 🇦🇪 Abu Dhabi If your clients are funds, asset managers or private banks, I’d put Abu Dhabi on your list. ADGM had 190 fund and asset managers by mid 2026. That’s a market worth getting to know if you recruit investment teams or specialise in legal search for funds and financial services firms. I’d also look at Abu Dhabi if you recruit the people who build and run data centres. With projects like Stargate UAE, experience across power, mechanical and electrical engineering, construction or commissioning is particularly relevant. 🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia If you’ve spent years running an energy or engineering contract desk and the bit you love most is winning business, look at Saudi. In the Eastern Province, we’re seeing agencies hire contract recruiters into business development roles. That could be your next career move as well as your next overseas move. Asia 🇭🇰 Hong Kong If you took Hong Kong off your list a few years ago, put it back on. Our clients are hiring expat recruiters again, especially for specialist desks in insurance, banking and financial services that work with international clients across Asia. Mandarin or Cantonese can give you an edge on desks that also cover mainland China. 🇸🇬 Singapore I’d look at Singapore if you want to run a genuinely regional desk. Think placing commercial leaders across Southeast Asia or working with international law firms and in-house legal teams across several markets. The Employment Pass salary threshold goes up for new applications in January 2027, so it’s worth checking where you stand early. 🇲🇾 Kuala Lumpur KL deserves more attention. It’s a great place to live as an expat, it’s very affordable, and I’d put it on the list if you recruit in tech or data centres. That includes the engineering and project teams that build and run them. KL is also home to regional business hubs, so you could live in Malaysia and run a desk that covers Southeast Asia. Some of the best moves I’ve helped recruiters make started with, “I’m curious, but I don’t know where I’d go.” If that’s you and you’re thinking about 2027, drop us a message. No CV needed. Tell us what you recruit and what you’d love from a move, and we’ll tell you where we’d look first. SJ Rec2Rec | Katie Wheeler Felix Fanshawe Keir Oakes Nikheta Gokuldas

posts.text: Deloitte Access Economics says data centres now make up $141 billion of Australia's construction pipeline, up 36% in a year. Its Investment Monitor puts the whole pipeline at a record $1.39 trillion, and it expects the value of work under construction to be near $870 billion in 2027, more than double the peak of the 2012 mining boom. What caught my eye was its point that data centres are competing with housing and infrastructure for the same people and materials near the big cities. Data Centres Australia said last week that capacity under construction has doubled since April, so a lot of this is being built now. I think that changes what a good Construction Director looks like. Delivering the halls safely, on time and on budget is still the job, but more of it now comes down to keeping a site team and the subcontractors together when every other project nearby wants the same electricians and supervisors. In my experience the leaders who manage that are the ones people have followed from job to job, and they usually have a few trusted contractors who will turn up for them. So when a business is hiring a senior construction lead, I'd ask the candidates who would come with them and which contractors would take their call, as well as what they've built. If you've hired a construction lead this year, how much did that count in the final decision? #DataCentres #Construction #Leadership

posts.text: I was chatting with a leasing manager in Hong Kong last week who had just moved roles. She mentioned that three of the four interviews she had involved some discussion of AI tools or data platforms, even though the roles themselves were still core leasing and asset management. The same pattern came up in a conversation with a facilities engineer in Singapore the week before. Traditional real estate skills remain essential, but candidates who can speak to how technology is changing day-to-day operations are getting more traction. Tech hiring continues to move, with AI-related mentions in job ads having more than tripled in Singapore since early 2024 and running even higher in Hong Kong. Backend, project and AI engineering roles are consistently active, while in real estate we continue to see steady demand for leasing, asset and facilities professionals who can work alongside those tools. The markets are not exploding, but selective hiring is happening for people who bring both commercial or technical depth and a practical understanding of how Asia’s property and tech sectors are evolving. posts.text: [Government Recruitment Workflow] Waiting half a year from submitting your application to receiving an offer? Unpacking the lengthy approval process and a "Waiting List" survival guide.【政府工招聘流程】由遞表到收Offer等足半年？拆解漫長審批程序與「Waiting List」生存指南🥵😤😖🥶😰🤢! CTgoodjobs' Editor Published: 2026-11-17 (1). In Hong Kong's job market, "government jobs" have long been synonymous with an "iron rice bowl." Backed by a stable pay structure, a clear promotion ladder, and comprehensive medical and leave benefits, they attract tens of thousands of applicants every year. However, many professionals accustomed to the fast-paced, decisive hiring rhythm of the private sector often feel at a loss when applying for Civil Service or Non-Civil Service Contract (NCSC) positions, where the recruitment process routinely drags on for several months—or even over half a year. Some candidates hear nothing at all after an interview, while others receive a bittersweet notification placing them on a "Waiting List." Without further ado, drawing on my background as a former Human Resources Practitioner and my current role as a career platform editor, I will break down the vetting mechanisms behind government recruitment and share a practical survival strategy for the waiting period, helping you map out your job search with greater clarity. 在香港職場, 「政府工」向來被視為「鐵飯碗」的代名詞，憑藉穩定的薪酬架構、清晰的晉升階梯以及完善的醫療和假期福利, 每年均吸引數以萬計的求職者投考. 然而, 不少習慣了私人市場「快狠準」招聘節奏的打工仔, 在投考公務員或非公務員合約（NCSC）職位時, 往往會對其動輒數個月甚至超過半年的招聘流程感到無所適從. 甚至有人在面試後石沉大海, 或收到一封令人又愛又恨的「候補名單（Waiting List）」通知書. 事不宜遲, 今天我便以曾任職人力資源從業員及現職求職平台編輯的角度, 為大家深入拆解政府工背後的審批機制, 並提供一套實用的候補期生存策略, 希望大家可以更清晰地規劃自己的求職路向！ TOOLS for solving this issue to be quoted. Unpacking the Lengthy Approval Process and a "Waiting List" Survival Guide.【政府工招聘流程】由遞表到收Offer等足半年？拆解漫長審批程序與「Waiting List」生存指南🥵😤😖🥶😰🤢! CTgoodjobs' Editor Published: 2026-11-17 (2). Applying continuous improvement and problem-solving methodologies to Hong Kong Civil Service/Government recruitment (cutting a 6+ month hiring cycle down without compromising statutory fairness or integrity vetting) is a classic transactional process optimization case. Below is a structured breakdown of how Lean Six Sigma, Theory of Constraints (TOC), TRIZ, Design Thinking, and 5W1H can be systematically deployed to eliminate waste, break bottlenecks, and accelerate time-to-hire. 1. Lean Six Sigma (DMAIC and Value Stream Mapping). In government hiring, 90%+ of the 6-month lead time is pure waiting time (Non-Value-Added waste) rather than actual interviewing or vetting time. Value Stream Mapping (VSM) and "DOWNTIME" Waste Elimination: Waiting (The #1 Culprit): Batch-processing applications (waiting until the application deadline closes before screening a single resume) creates massive queue delays. Solution: Switch to rolling screening for high-volume grades. Over-processing: Requiring every applicant to submit certified copies of academic transcripts at the initial application stage. Solution: Only require document verification and vetting from shortlisted finalists (top 5–10%), drastically reducing administrative checking hours. Defects (Rework): Incomplete forms or missing Basic Law/National Security Law test scores cause back-and-forth email delays. Solution: Embed Poka-Yoke (mistake-proofing) validation rules into the online portal so incomplete applications cannot be submitted. Parallel Processing (Concurrent Engineering): Instead of running Interview → Medical Exam → Integrity/Security Vetting → Reference Check sequentially, execute medical checks, reference verification, and security vetting simultaneously immediately after conditional offer issuance. posts.text: The Paradox of Paradoxes in Public Law A professor at the The University of Hong Kong (HKU)—paid by taxpayers—publicly promotes her private academic coaching service by drawing on her experience with search committees. She tells applicants that committees don't always pick the strongest person on paper, but instead pick people they have already met "over coffee". Yet the moment someone points out that this is illegal favoritism for a public servant, a corporate lawyer jumps into the comments to defend her. His argument? That she was "posting in her personal capacity" and might just be sharing "hearsay she heard from other people" rather than talking about HKU! Think about how absurd that defense is: to save a taxpayer-funded professor from admitting to patronage at her own university, her defenders have to claim she is charging coaching clients for third-hand rumors. This exposes the biggest paradox of the British and Hong Kong common-law system: On one hand, Hong Kong law classifies public university professors as public servants, where favoring friends over the best candidates on paper is a serious crime called Misconduct in Public Office. Across most of Asia—including Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, and Thailand—strict anti-corruption and civil service laws make it completely illegal for public university faculty to run private side-businesses coaching people on how to bypass meritocracy through informal coffee meetings. On the other hand, common-law culture protects insiders with word games and massive financial walls. In Hong Kong, an elite can use their public university title to sell private coaching, and if you challenge them, lawyers simply say, "Prove in the High Court that she didn't mean somewhere else—and if you lose, you pay the university’s massive legal bills." Compare that to a developing country like Thailand, which uses administrative law: Under the Thai Constitution and Administrative Court system, challenging public-sector corruption is 100% free. You don't have to play word games with expensive lawyers about what a professor "really meant." Any citizen can ask the Administrative Court or Thailand’s anti-corruption commissions (NACC and PACC) to subpoena the exact scoring sheets and records of every hiring and tenure committee that professor has ever sat on—for free—to verify if weaker candidates were pushed forward. Wealthy common-law jurisdictions love to lecture the world about the "Rule of Law." Yet in practice, their system uses plausible deniability and terrifying court costs to shield powerful insiders, while Thailand’s administrative law simply opens the files and checks the evidence. People online treat this as "common sense" career advice. Only privileged applicants can afford expensive international flights, conference fees, and private coaches. Researchers from poorer backgrounds get shut out simply because they cannot afford to buy access to the insider club.

posts.text: ADB is hiring: DIGITAL SECTOR ADVISOR TA-10823 REG: Pacific Private Sector Development Initiative, Phase V - DIGITAL SECTOR ADVISOR (E-058359-001) Objective and Purpose of the Assignment The Pacific Private Sector Development Initiative (PSDI) is a regional technical assistance facility co‑financed by the Government of Australia, the Government of New Zealand, and the Asian Development Bank (ADB). Since 2006, PSDI has supported Pacific Developing Member Countries (DMCs) to improve the enabling environment for business and promote inclusive, private sector‑led economic growth. The Digital Sector Advisor will support PSDI Phase V to strengthen digital transformation across business regulation, public administration, and financial systems. The advisor will work closely with the Business Law Reform Lead and the Financial Sector Lead to ensure that digital solutions—particularly business registries, beneficial ownership systems, and digital finance platforms—are well‑designed, interoperable, secure, and appropriate for Pacific contexts. The advisor will also help PSDI understand and address the gender‑differentiated opportunities and constraints associated with digital government and digital finance, including barriers faced by women and people with disabilities in accessing and using digital technologies. Scope of Work The assignment will be a part-time position that will focus on supporting PSDI technical leads in integrating issues relating to digitalization into PSDI’s support for private sector development in the Pacific region. This includes: Advising on the design and implementation of digital business registries, beneficial ownership systems, and related e‑government platforms. Ensuring digital solutions integrate effectively with broader ADB and development partner digital government initiatives. Supporting the development of digital finance ecosystems, including fintech‑enabled services, digital payments, and alternative financing platforms. Assessing digital inclusion challenges—particularly for women, MSMEs, and people with disabilities—and advising on strategies to ensure equitable access to digital services. Providing technical guidance on interoperability, data standards, cybersecurity, user‑centred design, and long‑term sustainability of digital systems. Supporting PSDI’s monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) and knowledge work related to digital transformation. The advisor will be engaged on request. A Technical Lead identifies the need, normally at concept note stage, and the PSDI Team Leader agrees the scope and days. The cross-cutting advisers will contribute to a single screen of concept notes with the Economic Empowerment of Women Lead Expert, so Technical Leads receive one consolidated review.

posts.text: Wanted: A Deity in Work Boots. Must have 5 years experience, know CAD, and accept mid-tier project engineer wages. I ran across a job posting today that reads less like a job search and more like an AI prompt fed an entire freshman textbook on Construction Management, told to "include every noun you can think of," and then slapped with a price tag from 2004. SUSHISAMBA is looking for a "Senior Project Manager" to drive their global luxury hospitality expansion. The salary band? $100,000 to $120,000. Let’s unpack what they expect in exchange for that entry-level consulting rate: The Real Estate Mogul: Pre-lease due diligence, site evaluation, and negotiating international lease terms with institutional landlords across London, Vegas, Milan, and Singapore. The Senior Architect & Specifier: Directing design teams, drawing details, reviewing shop submittals, drafting elevations, and oh—"CAD skills a plus." (Because obviously, between international lease negotiations, you’ll be drafting millwork details, duh). The Chief Estimator & CapEx Director: Strategic capital allocation, portfolio cash flow forecasting, multi-million-dollar VE exercises, and managing $5M to $20M+ concurrent domestic and global buildouts. The Municipal Code Whisperer: Navigating plan checks, entitlements, and permitting across multiple international sovereign jurisdictions. The Field Super / CA Grind: Crawling the site, answering RFIs, resolving trade clashes, handling supplier logistics, and hashing out subcontractor change orders in the dirt. All of this, mind you, for a global portfolio spanning the UK, the Middle East, the US, and Asia. This isn't a job listing. It’s an inventory of terms written by a committee that knows a restaurant requires walls and money, but hasn't the foggiest idea how either gets managed. When you ask for an Owner's Rep, a Corporate Development Director, an Architect of Record, a Lead Estimator, a Field Super, and a Contract Attorney—and you package it into one human being for $110k—you aren’t hiring a Senior PM. You’re hiring an inevitable catastrophic failure and suggesting the vision plan is included. In luxury hospitality, a single mismanaged kitchen exhaust interface or an overlooked landlord work letter clause will burn through $120,000 before the concrete cures. If you treat the person protecting your balance sheet as a low-bid commodity, the field will teach you the difference between cost and value in the most painful way possible. If you find the person who actually possesses all of these skills, can execute them simultaneously across five time zones, and takes this role for $105k... check their references. Because you didn't hire a unicorn. You hired someone who memorized the syllabus. #HospitalityDevelopment #CommercialConstruction #OwnersRepresentative #CapitalPrograms #ProjectManagement #RealityCheck

posts.text: #hiring First Product Hire - Enterprise AI Product Manager Apply here: [link hidden] First product hireDevelop and own the product roadmapBuild enterprise grade AI solutionsProduct ManagerSydney or Melbourne, remote-first$180,000 to $200,000 plus superSpikewerks is an enterprise AI company building spikeOS, a platform that lets large regulated organisations use AI on information they can actually trust.The problem is a familiar one. The information that matters within a big business sits in four places that do not talk to each other: market data, documents such as contracts and statements, operational systems, and the spreadsheets people work in every day. A data warehouse joins up the numbers and leaves the documents behind. A language model pointed at a folder of PDFs can read them, but it cannot calculate or show where an answer came from.spikeOS sits in between. It reads from all four sources, extracts the facts, and stores them as structured records, with every field linking back to the page or reading it came from. Nothing is written without an owners approval.The company is live in two industries. Energy, working with generators, asset owners and retailers. And lending, through a partnership with a loan management platform that reaches a large share of Australias non-bank lenders.The roleThis is the first product hire at Spikewerks.spikeOS becomes useful to an industry through a domain pack: the standard version of the product for that sector, covering the data it works with, the systems it connects to, the checks that matter in that industry and the outputs it produces. Lending has a pack. Energy is getting one.The Product Manager owns them. What goes in, in what order, and what gets declined.That last part is the job. With engineers going into the field and new clients starting from the packs, someone has to decide what becomes standard and what stays with one customer. Without that, the product becomes the sum of every clients request.The role reports to the CEO and works alongside the CTO, writing the requirements directly: extraction logic, rule libraries, evaluation sets. The CTO reviews them and owns how they get built.What Spikewerks is looking forA product manager who writes technical specifications. Data models, interface specs, rules, how accuracy gets measuredExperience in B2B or enterprise productA roadmap that reflects a view of where the product should go, rather than a queue of customer requestsThe confidence to say no, including to a paying customerExperience with document extraction, RAG, rules engines or applied AI in a regulated setting is attractive, as is an engineering or data background earlier in their career.Things to knowSpikewerks is early. There is no product roadmap to inherit, which is both the challenge and the opportunity. The team is small and growing quickly. This is a first-ten hire with direct access to the founders. Apply Now

posts.text: I'm now an Australian Permanent Resident! 🇦🇺 It's been a long year. I moved to Australia in 2019 to study Interaction Design at UTS, then spent almost 4 years working as a product designer. Last October, after almost 6.5 years there, my 485 graduate visa ended, and I had to leave. Two weeks later, I got my PR invite. The timing could've been better. I applied in December and had to wait offshore. It was meant to take 3 to 6 months, so I planned to use that time to build my skills and spend time with my family. Then processing kept getting longer, and not knowing when it would come through was honestly stressful. In the meantime, I did some freelance work, rebuilt my portfolio, and spent most of my time learning to design and build with AI. That turned into Procap, a tool to record your product and polish the video after. I took it from an idea to a public waitlist on my own: procap.app I'm heading back and looking for a product design role in Australia. If you're hiring or know someone who is, let me know. Any Malaysian company advertising for a "Creative Designer" should be legally required to disclose how many departments they're actually trying to hire. Graphic design? One. Video editing? Two. Motion graphics? Three. Copywriting, photography, social media management, content strategy, event coverage, and occasionally being the office's unofficial IT department? Congratulations. You're not hiring a designer. You're assembling an agency with one salary. And somehow, the job description still ends with: "Must be passionate, creative, and willing to work under pressure." Passion has become the industry's favourite substitute for a proper budget. Here's the uncomfortable part. We keep celebrating Malaysia's creative potential while treating creative professionals like interchangeable production tools. We want international-standard work with local-budget expectations. We praise originality until someone presents an idea we haven't seen before. We demand strategic thinking, then measure a designer's worth by how quickly they can finish 20 social media posters. And when talented creatives eventually leave, burn out, or start charging properly? Suddenly, they're "difficult to work with." Perhaps the Malaysian creative industry doesn't need another motivational conference about unlocking creativity. Perhaps it needs to learn the difference between hiring a creative professional and purchasing unlimited access to their labour. Creativity is not an unlimited resource, and passion is not a payment method.

posts.text: The best web designer I know runs a terrible agency. Not because he’s bad at design. Because he’s brilliant at it. If you started your business because you were good at the work, this post is going to sting a little. Thursday evening, your customer hands you another revision. And you think: “I could do this myself.” That thought has killed more businesses than any recession. Michael Gerber calls it the Entrepreneurial Seizure in The E-Myth Revisited. A designer, an engineer, a lawyer, a chef, a good technician gets fed up and decides to go out on their own. And in that moment, they make what Gerber calls the fatal assumption: “If I understand the technical work, I understand the business that does the technical work.” They don’t. Neither did I. Here’s what nobody tells you on that Thursday evening. The work you’re good at is maybe 30% of the business. The other 70% is the part you’ve never done: → Finding clients before you need them → Pricing so that you can actually pay yourself → Chasing payments without damaging the relationship → Managing scope when the client says “small change only” → Hiring, and then trusting what you’ve hired → Building systems so the work doesn’t depend on you Nobody taught you that. You were busy being good at the work. So what happens? You go from being a designer to being a designer who also does sales, admin, accounts and customer service. At midnight. For less money than you made before. You didn’t start a business. You bought yourself a job. With a worse boss. I’ve watched this happen to talented people in Malaysia over and over. Great engineers running struggling engineering firms. Brilliant creatives who can’t keep an agency afloat. The skill was never the problem. The problem is the seizure comes with no plan for the other 70%. If you’re about to take the leap, do this first: 1. Admit the business is a different skill from the craft. Treat it like one you have to learn. 2. Decide on day one what the business will look like without you in it. Then work towards that. 3. Spend at least one day a week working on the business, not in it. Protect it like a client meeting. Write down how you do things, even when it’s just you. The system you document today is the staff member you can hire tomorrow. The leap isn’t the mistake. Taking it with only your technical skills is. If you’ve made the leap, what did you wish you’d known that first year? Connect for more stories: Clement Chwin Chiat Ng of Rebrand Malaysia

posts.text: "𝐉𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐨, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭." That's our advice to overseas businesses hiring Filipino web developers and designers. Finding talent here isn't the hard part. Knowing what to check is. What the market pays (Indeed Philippines averages, 2026, at ₱62.50 = US$1): → Web developer: ₱35,055 a month (about US$561) → WordPress developer: ₱39,300 (about US$629) → Full-stack developer: ₱55,828 (about US$893) → Web designer: ₱29,685 (about US$475) Those are averages, not quotes. A senior specialist working your hours should earn well above them. If a quote looks too cheap for the skill you need, it usually is. Language is rarely the issue. The Philippines ranked 28th on the EF English Proficiency Index 2025. A vague brief is the real problem. And Manila runs just 2–3 hours behind Sydney and Melbourne, so most of the workday overlaps. How we'd hire: 1. A WordPress or Shopify specialist over a generalist. Most small businesses don't need full-stack. 2. A paid 1–2 day trial. Unpaid "test projects" put off the best people. 3. Domain, hosting, admin and code in your business's name, with copyright assigned in writing. The developer worth paying explains how your site will win more enquiries, not how many languages they know. What's the one thing you test before hiring a developer? I've always believed that skills can be taught, but attitude and life experience are a different matter. People who've faced significant challenges in life can bring so much to the workplace. Resilience, determination, resourcefulness and often a completely different way of looking at things. And that's something I think businesses underestimate. Someone looking at a challenge through a different set of eyes might just come up with a brilliant idea or a better way of doing something that nobody else had thought of. That's how businesses grow too! Throughout my career I've seen what happens when people are given an opportunity, trusted and supported to develop (and I've been fortunate enough to have been given that chance myself when life wasn't looking too good!) I do wonder whether we sometimes get so caught up in someone's qualifications and previous experience that we miss the person and their potential. After all, isn't that part of being a great leader? Seeing what someone could become, rather than just what they've done so far. I suspect there's some extraordinary talent out there that simply doesn't come wrapped in the CV we're expecting! … more

To be fair, the JD does mention product-suite ownership, business economics and platform thinking. But as a candidate, I'd still ask: “Which specific product or product suite will I own in my first 6 months?” A very reasonable question before investing time in the process.
My favourite JD decoding rule: If you cannot identify the customer, product boundary and success metric, don't start tailoring your resume yet. First understand what you're applying for. 😂
This is the difference between applying to a job title and positioning for an actual mandate. That's what I help PMs decode through personalised JD X-RAY sessions. 📌 [link hidden]

The "own a suite of products" line is the tell — when a JD can't name the product, the scope is whatever's on fire that quarter. The question I always had to ask a recruiter was who actually owns the P&L and the roadmap call, because "cross-functional leadership" in a JD usually means you get the accountability without the authority. Your four-point checklist is the right filter; I'd add a fifth — who can say no to a request and make it stick. In my experience, that's the difference between a PM and a very well-paid order-taker.

[name hidden] Ryan, that fifth question is gold. 👏 Accountability without decision authority is one of the biggest traps hidden inside senior PM roles. I'd go one step further: Who has the final call when priorities conflict, and who backs that decision? Because a PM's real mandate isn't measured by how many things they own, but by the decisions they're empowered to make. 🎯

What will MasterCard do when Visa Network has ICICI onboarded from so long ? MasteCard issued HDFC ? And the Rupay network is prepaid as well as credit card our very own and set up with UPI and NPCI in mind ? What is MasterCard trying to achieve ?
That repeat visit point is the real test, Bhawana. A product parents trust once is the one they come back to without thinking.

👉The phrase I'd investigate in this JD: “Partner with worldwide Payments, Subscriptions, Personalization and App Experience teams.” My question: Who owns the final trade-off when local customer needs conflict with global platform priorities? That's where the real mandate becomes visible.

✅️ A useful interview question: “Which decisions can this PM make independently, which require global alignment, and which are owned by another product team?” Three answers. Three very different operating models.

📍Here's the candidate exercise: A local payment method improves conversion in India but adds complexity to a global payments platform. What would you evaluate before prioritising it? Customer value. Conversion. Cost. Reuse. Operational complexity. That's the product judgement behind the job title.

dataHash.scope: Canonical sorted-key UTF-8 JSON of {posts,comments}, compact separators

hashes.recordsScope: Canonical sorted-key UTF-8 JSON of {posts,comments}, compact separators

ageCoverage.definition: ageDays is exposure at collection, not age as of today. Exact source dates and dates derived from relative labels are separated.

analysisRule.expression: !isDuplicate && rawSourceTextLength >= 80 && likes !== null && commentsCount !== null && batch !== 'B7'
analysisRule.textLengthBasis: Original CSV post_text before anonymisation; whitespace counted, matching legacy builder.

meta.textFeaturePolicy: All six current text features are recalculated by the browser's current rules from the anonymised full text, rather than copied from the legacy five-signal aggregates. Link presence alone does not establish an application path. Regex coding needs human review.

datePolicy.exact: Source post_time, compared with collected_at at calendar-day precision.
datePolicy.relative: Parsed minute/hour/day/week time_label. ageDays is retained; publishedAt remains null because the exact date/time is unknown.
datePolicy.missing: No usable observation; no date or age is invented. LI00030 has a source publication date one day after collection; both age and publication date are suppressed.
datePolicy.commentCollectedAt: Inherited from linked post collection timestamp; comment export has no collection timestamp. Unlinked comments remain null.

privacy.policy: No author fields. Known author/commenter names, emails, phone candidates, body URLs and contact handles are replaced. Only LinkedIn source-post URLs are retained in url. No text truncation.
privacy.salaryPolicy: Currency amounts, pay-unit amounts, and unlabelled four-plus-digit salary ranges are preserved when not explicitly phone-labelled.

limitations: Convenience sample of visible public LinkedIn hiring-related posts; not representative of the labour market.
Visible likes and comments are observations at collection, not applicants, hires, reach, or causal hiring effectiveness.
Different posting ages, occupations, search lanes, and collection batches can confound engagement comparisons.
Comment rows are the collected visible comment layer, not all comments counted by LinkedIn; five empty bodies remain present.
Source post_text can itself be clipped by the captured public page; this export preserves all supplied text and adds no length truncation.
Posts without LinkedIn links remain in the snapshot; their source page cannot be opened from the supplied master data.
Automated regex job families and text signals are coding aids and may contain classification error.
Redaction can affect text-signal detection; original contact values are intentionally unavailable to the public browser dataset.
All current text features use anonymised text and current browser rules; link presence alone does not establish an application path, and rule matches need human review.
Seven newly supplied rows could not pass the website validation rules and remain excluded from the bundled working baseline.

The finance and insurance import contains 85 approved posts and 44 linked comments from a 160-candidate batch. Search URLs requested the past month, but the collection summary could not confirm that filter automatically for every query.
The public-sector/non-profit import added 67 dated posts derived from confirmed LinkedIn post IDs and 49 linked comments; one unique candidate without a confirmed source ID was excluded.

The retail/logistics CSV contained 1,000 rows; 986 passed validation, including 297 retail/e-commerce posts and 689 logistics/transportation posts. Six records without a verifiable publication date and eight duplicate rows were excluded.

The 2026-11-20 working baseline merges the original frozen sample with the education, manufacturing, construction, real-estate, hospitality, operations/administration, healthcare, finance/insurance, public-sector/non-profit, retail/e-commerce and logistics/transportation collections.

The complete healthcare collection contains 500 raw records. 434 passed the export quality rules and were considered for website import; 351 were new after website deduplication, 80 duplicated existing records, and 3 newer snapshots were not applied because they would reclassify existing construction or hospitality posts. Only 83 imported records have complete interaction fields; 57 of the 434 import rows lack a usable URL, and 351 lack at least one interaction count.

The 2026-11-21 supplementary batches added 1436 posts from construction, public sector/non-profit, product/project management and design searches. The supplements are convenience samples with missing interaction fields preserved; category completion is reported separately from raw collection targets.
